purpose: Compact first-pass article search directory. Load this before full article-registry or article content refs.

articles.title: Analytics: add provider
articles.oneLineSummary: Explains how to add a new analytics destination from the Integrations Analytics area. It covers opening the provider picker, selecting tools such as Google Analytics 4, Google Tag Manager, Meta Pixel, TikTok Pixel, Amplitude, Mixpanel, PostHog, custom scripts, or server-side destinations, then publishing and verifying events.

subarticles.title: Add a destination
subarticles.summary: Use Add to open the provider picker, then choose from 15+ client and server platforms (Amplitude, GA4, GTM, Mixpanel, PostHog, Facebook Pixel, TikTok Pixel, custom scripts, and server-side variants).

subarticles.title: Publish and verify
subarticles.summary: After saving, publish a test Web Placement and watch the provider dashboard for incoming events (page views, screen changes, actions, checkout steps). If nothing arrives within 30 seconds, recheck the ID or token.

articles.title: Analytics integration list
articles.oneLineSummary: Explains how to review the Analytics integrations list before launch. It covers checking which destinations are enabled, removing stale tracking IDs, understanding that enabled integrations inject into published web funnels, and enabling Segmently first-party analytics for internal reports and canvas insights.

subarticles.title: Disable or remove stale destinations
subarticles.summary: Before testing, turn off destinations that are no longer needed or use outdated tracking IDs. This keeps validation results clean and avoids polluting old analytics accounts.

subarticles.title: Review active destinations
subarticles.summary: This list shows every configured destination and whether it is enabled. Each enabled integration injects automatically into every published web funnel.

subarticles.title: Enable Segmently Analytics (internal reporting)
subarticles.summary: Segmently Analytics is the first-party provider behind Segmently Reports and canvas insights. Add and enable it to collect funnel events for reporting and optimization; it is disabled by default.

articles.title: Analytics provider configuration
articles.oneLineSummary: Explains provider-specific analytics configuration fields and validation. It covers integration names, GA4 Measurement IDs, GTM Container IDs, Amplitude, Mixpanel, PostHog, Meta Pixel, TikTok Pixel, custom HEAD or BODY scripts, server-side Conversions API style destinations, and how to verify events after saving.

subarticles.title: Amplitude: API key and server zone
subarticles.summary: Paste the API Key from your Amplitude project Settings, then pick the server zone (US, or EU for GDPR data residency) that matches where your Amplitude project lives — the wrong zone means events never arrive. You can also turn on session start/end tracking to capture session lifecycle events.

subarticles.title: Custom Script: HEAD and BODY
subarticles.summary: For tools without a built-in option, add your own JavaScript at two points: code in HEAD runs before the page renders (load SDKs here), and code in BODY runs after it loads (attach handlers here). Call window.segmentlySDK.setCustomData(key, value) to hand funnel data to your script. Reach for this only when no built-in provider above fits.

subarticles.title: Facebook (Meta) Pixel: Pixel ID
subarticles.summary: Paste the Pixel ID from Meta Events Manager so your funnel and checkout events attribute back to your Facebook and Instagram ad campaigns. Optionally turn on auto-config to also capture button clicks and page metadata without extra setup.

subarticles.title: Google Analytics 4: Measurement ID
subarticles.summary: Paste your Measurement ID (it looks like G-XXXXXXXXXX). Find it in GA4 under Admin then Data Streams then your web stream. It routes every funnel event to the correct GA4 property; if the format is wrong, Segmently blocks the save so a typo can't silently break tracking.

subarticles.title: Google Tag Manager: Container ID
subarticles.summary: Paste your Container ID (it looks like GTM-XXXXX) from Google Tag Manager. Segmently pushes every funnel event into the dataLayer, so your existing GTM triggers and tags fire on them. Only set a custom Data Layer name if your container was specifically built to expect a non-default one.

subarticles.title: Name the integration
subarticles.summary: Enter a clear label such as 'GA4 Production' or 'Amplitude EU'. It only appears in your own integrations list and edit menus to help you tell destinations apart — visitors never see it. Pick a name that says which tool and which environment it points at.

subarticles.title: Mixpanel: project token
subarticles.summary: Paste the Project Token from your Mixpanel project Settings, then choose where it's stored on the visitor's browser (localStorage by default, or Cookie if your setup needs it). You can also enable page-view tracking if you want each screen view recorded automatically.

subarticles.title: PostHog: project token and region
subarticles.summary: Paste the Project Token — that's the API key, not the numeric Project ID — found in PostHog under Settings then General. Then pick your region: US Cloud, EU Cloud, or Self-Hosted. If you chose Self-Hosted, also enter your own PostHog API host URL so events know where to go.

subarticles.title: Server-side analytics (Conversions API, GA4 Measurement Protocol, and more)
subarticles.summary: Server-side destinations send payment events straight from Segmently's servers — purchase, subscription, cancellation, and failure only — for revenue attribution that ad-blockers and browser limits can't drop. They use the same credentials as the matching client pixel but do not receive engagement events (screen views, button taps), so run them alongside the client pixel to track the full funnel.

subarticles.title: TikTok Pixel: Pixel ID
subarticles.summary: Paste the Pixel ID (it looks like CXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX) from TikTok Ads Manager under Events. Under Advanced Matching you can optionally pass hashed email and phone, which improves how reliably TikTok attributes conversions back to your ads.

articles.title: Collect the customer email before the paywall (required for subscriptions)
articles.oneLineSummary: Explains why a paid subscription funnel must collect the visitor email before the paywall and how that email supports Stripe subscriptions, customer identity, receipts, attribution, and later billing support. Use this for questions about email capture before checkout, subscription readiness, and metadata needed before showing a paywall.

articles.title: Send Facebook (CAPI) events from your web funnel
articles.oneLineSummary: Shows how to turn on Facebook Conversions API (CAPI) event forwarding for a web funnel: open the Edit Web Funnel dialog, and in the Destinations section click the one-click + Facebook CAPI button, which adds the visitor IP, user agent, and Facebook _fbp and _fbc cookies to both Server Data and Stripe Metadata, then publish. Use this when a customer asks how to pass or send Facebook events from their funnel, enable Facebook CAPI attribution, forward fbp/fbc, or improve Meta ad match quality on purchases. Connecting the Pixel ID and access token is a separate prerequisite covered by the Facebook Pixel and Conversion API setup guide.

articles.title: Every event Segmently sends to Facebook (Pixel + Conversions API)
articles.oneLineSummary: Lists the Facebook Pixel and Conversions API events that Segmently can send from a funnel, including page visits, onboarding interactions, product catalog selection, checkout, and purchase-related signals. Use this when customers ask what Facebook or Meta events are emitted, which parameters are included, or how the event catalog relates to attribution and optimization.

articles.title: Set up the Facebook (Meta) Pixel and Conversion API
articles.oneLineSummary: Shows how to connect Facebook or Meta analytics to Segmently by adding the Pixel ID and Conversions API token, then verifying that funnel events can be sent to Meta. Use this for setup questions about Facebook Pixel, Meta Pixel, CAPI, access tokens, provider configuration, and event tracking readiness.

articles.oneLineSummary: Documents the Action Bar section that controls the screen's primary and secondary call-to-action buttons. It covers button labels, text styles, fill and border styling, gradients, shadows, effects, icons, spacing, and which screens use the shared bottom button bar, including WebEmbed and ordinary onboarding screens.

subarticles.title: Action Bar — every setting
subarticles.summary: The bottom button bar — your primary call-to-action and an optional secondary button. This guide documents every setting of the Action Bar block, grouped by area. Each setting matches a real control in the screen editor.

subarticles.title: Action Bar section
subarticles.summary: The Action Bar holds the screen's main call-to-action: the primary button (like Continue) and an optional secondary button. This is the control that actually moves visitors forward, so set its label to match what happens next and make sure it points to the same screen you connected on the canvas. It shows on most interactive screens; if a screen has no continuation button, add the next step from the canvas instead.

subarticles.title: Where it appears
subarticles.summary: Covered screen types: HeroContent, ListMultiPick, ListSinglePick, GridMultiPick, GridSinglePick, TextInput, WheelPicker, HeroList, WebEmbed.

subarticles.title: Main button shape and fill
subarticles.summary: Sets the main button's look — background color, border, corner radius, height, inner padding, and a full-width toggle. For an ad landing page keep it full-width and high-contrast so it reads as the obvious next step. The Visibility toggle hides the button entirely; only hide it when the screen forces a choice first, and never hide both buttons.

subarticles.title: Motion on the main button
subarticles.summary: Optional animation for the call-to-action — pulse, glow, bounce, scale, fade-in, slide-up and more, plus an opacity control. A gentle pulse or glow can draw the eye and lift taps; save attention-grabbing effects for your key conversion screen and avoid stacking several. Leave it off for a calm, professional feel.

subarticles.title: Gradient on the main button
subarticles.summary: An optional color gradient layered over the button's solid fill — set start and end colors, the angle, extra color stops, and an optional moving shimmer. Leave it off for a clean flat look; turn it on to make the call-to-action pop against a busy background. Keep enough contrast that the label stays easy to read.

subarticles.title: Icon on the main button
subarticles.summary: An optional icon next to the label — choose start or end placement, size, corner radius, and spacing, and how it fits its box (fit shows the whole icon, fill crops to cover). A small leading arrow or lock icon can reinforce the action; keep it in the same color family as the label. Leave it empty for a clean text-only button.

subarticles.title: Main button label
subarticles.summary: The text on your main call-to-action button — the one that moves visitors to the next screen. Make it a short, specific verb phrase tied to the action (Continue, Get my plan, Subscribe) rather than a generic word; clear, benefit-led labels lift click-through on a paid landing page. This text can be translated per language.

subarticles.title: Shadow under the main button
subarticles.summary: An optional drop shadow beneath the button, with control over its color, blur, and vertical drop. A soft shadow lifts the call-to-action off the page so it feels tappable; keep it subtle (low blur, small offset) so it looks intentional rather than heavy. Leave it off if your theme is flat.

subarticles.title: Main button text style
subarticles.summary: Typography for the main button label — font, weight, size, color, and alignment. Leave it on the theme defaults for a consistent look; bump the weight or size, or switch color, only when the label is hard to read against the button fill. Applies to the label in every language.

subarticles.title: Secondary button shape and fill
subarticles.summary: Sets the secondary button's look — background, border, corner radius, height, padding, and a full-width toggle. Give it lower visual weight than the main button (an outline or transparent fill works well) so it doesn't compete with your call-to-action. The Visibility toggle hides it; never hide both the primary and secondary buttons.

subarticles.title: Motion on the secondary button
subarticles.summary: Adds optional movement to the secondary (lower-priority) button, such as pulse, glow, or bounce, plus an opacity control to fade it. Leave this off by default. Animation draws the eye, so reserve it for your main button only; making the alternative path move competes with your primary call to action and typically lowers conversions.

subarticles.title: Gradient on the secondary button
subarticles.summary: An optional color gradient over the secondary button's solid fill (start/end colors, angle, stops, optional shimmer). Usually leave this off — a gradient draws attention, which you want on your main call-to-action, not the side path. Turn it on only if a flat secondary clashes with your theme.

subarticles.title: Icon on the secondary button
subarticles.summary: An optional icon on the secondary button — placement (start or end), size, corner radius, spacing, and how it fits its box (fit shows the whole icon, fill crops to cover). Usually leave it empty so the secondary stays understated; add one only when it clarifies the action, like a back arrow for Go back.

subarticles.title: Secondary button label
subarticles.summary: Text for the optional second button — use it for a side path like Skip, Maybe later, or Restore purchase, never your main goal. On funnel steps an easy escape route can cost conversions, so leave it empty unless you genuinely need the alternative; on a paywall a low-key secondary is fine.

subarticles.title: Shadow under the secondary button
subarticles.summary: An optional drop shadow under the secondary button (color, blur, vertical drop). Keep it lighter than the main button's shadow, or off entirely, so the secondary stays visually subordinate to your call-to-action.

subarticles.title: Secondary button text style
subarticles.summary: Typography for the secondary button label — font, weight, size, color, and alignment. Style it deliberately quieter than the main button (lighter weight, muted color) so your primary call-to-action stays the obvious choice. Leave it on theme defaults unless the hierarchy looks off.

subarticles.summary: Stretch the button across the whole bar. Full-width reads as the obvious next step on a phone; turn it off for a button only as wide as its label.

subarticles.summary: Show or hide this button entirely. Never hide both buttons, or the screen has no way forward.

subarticles.title: • Width

subarticles.title: • Animation
subarticles.summary: An optional looping motion to draw the eye to the action — choose from None, Pulse, Shimmer, Bounce, Shake, Glow, Ripple, Scale, Fade In, Slide Up or Wiggle.

subarticles.title: • Enable effects
subarticles.summary: Off by default (gated on opacity). Turning it on sets the button to full opacity and a default Shimmer animation, then reveals the opacity slider and animation menu. (The animation choice is remembered but inactive while effects are off.)

subarticles.title: • Opacity
subarticles.summary: How see-through the whole button is, from 0% (invisible) to 100% (solid).

subarticles.title: Gradient on the main button
subarticles.summary: An optional color gradient layered over the button's solid fill — set start and end colors, the angle, extra color stops, and an optional moving shimmer. Leave it off for a clean flat look; turn it on to make the call-to-action pop against a busy background. Keep enough contrast that the label stays easy to read.

subarticles.title: Gradient on the main button
subarticles.summary: Gradient on the main button

subarticles.title: • Angle / direction
subarticles.summary: Which way the colors flow across the button. Medium offers preset directions (e.g. 90° left→right, 180° top→bottom); Advanced lets you type any angle from 0–360°.

subarticles.title: • Color stops (Advanced)
subarticles.summary: The full list of colors in the gradient. Add up to five stops and set each stop’s color and its position (0–100%) along the sweep, for multi-color blends beyond a simple two-color fade.

subarticles.title: • Detail level
subarticles.summary: A complexity switch (not saved on its own): Simple = just a start and end color; Medium = adds a direction angle and a shimmer toggle; Advanced = multi-stop colors plus a numeric angle, size and the full shimmer controls. Pick the depth you need.

subarticles.title: • Enable gradient
subarticles.summary: Off by default — the button uses a single flat color. Turn this on to blend colors across the fill for a richer look; turn it off for a clean solid button.

subarticles.title: • End color
subarticles.summary: The color the gradient fades to (the last color stop). Keep enough contrast with the start color that the label stays readable.

subarticles.title: • Gradient size (Advanced)
subarticles.summary: How far the gradient is stretched, from 50% (tight, punchy transition) to 200% (soft, gradual spread).

subarticles.title: • Shimmer
subarticles.summary: An optional animated sheen that sweeps across the button. When on you can tune the trigger (on hover, on a timer, or off), the streak color, its width and skew (slant), the duration of one sweep, and — for the timer trigger — the cycle gap between sweeps.

subarticles.title: • Start color
subarticles.summary: The color the gradient begins with (the first color stop / left-most stop in Advanced).

subarticles.title: Icon on the main button
subarticles.summary: An optional icon next to the label — choose start or end placement, size, corner radius, and spacing, and how it fits its box (fit shows the whole icon, fill crops to cover). A small leading arrow or lock icon can reinforce the action; keep it in the same color family as the label. Leave it empty for a clean text-only button.

subarticles.summary: Icon on the main button

subarticles.title: • Corner radius
subarticles.summary: Rounding of the icon’s corners in pixels; raise it to clip a square image into a rounded or circular badge.

subarticles.title: • Enable icon
subarticles.summary: Off by default. Turn on to show an image (icon) alongside the button label; off for a text-only button.

subarticles.title: • Height
subarticles.summary: The icon’s height in pixels (0–200).

subarticles.title: • Icon image
subarticles.summary: Upload an image file or paste an image URL — the icon shown next to the label. Leave empty to show no graphic.

subarticles.title: • Icon padding
subarticles.summary: The space around the icon (top, right, bottom, left) — the gap between the icon and the label and the button edges.

subarticles.title: • Placement
subarticles.summary: Where the icon sits relative to the label: Start (before the text) or End (after it); the Fixed Start/End variants pin it to the button’s left/right edge; Top and Bottom stack it above or below the label.

subarticles.title: • Scale mode
subarticles.summary: How the image fits its box: Scale to Fill (stretch), Aspect Fit (show the whole icon, may letterbox), Aspect Fill (cover the box, may crop), or Center (no resize).

subarticles.title: • Width
subarticles.summary: The icon’s width in pixels (0–200).

articles.title: Background
articles.oneLineSummary: Explains the Background section used across screen types to set the full-screen backdrop behind content. It covers solid color, photo, video, browser chrome color, visual contrast, and where background controls appear on regular screens, WebEmbed, Paywall, and Flexible Layout screens.

subarticles.title: Background section
subarticles.summary: Sets the full-screen backdrop behind everything on this screen — a solid color, a photo, or a looping video. It is the first thing a visitor sees, so match it to the theme and keep enough contrast for the header and buttons to stay readable.

subarticles.title: Where it appears
subarticles.summary: Covered screen types: HeroContent, Carousel, ListMultiPick, ListSinglePick, GridMultiPick, GridSinglePick, TextInput, WheelPicker, HeroList, WebEmbed, Paywall, FlexibleLayout.

subarticles.title: Tint The Phone's Top Bar
subarticles.summary: Sets the color of the surrounding system bars on web funnels, the strip at the top showing time and battery, and the bottom address bar. Leave it unset for almost every screen so it inherits your onboarding default. Set a color only when you want the phone's frame to blend into a full-bleed background for a seamless look.

subarticles.title: Full-Screen Background Photo
subarticles.summary: Uploads an image that fills the screen background when the background is set to Photo. It scales to cover the whole screen, so edges can get cropped on different phone sizes, keep your focal point centered. If you put text on top, choose a darker or dimmed image so your copy stays readable.

subarticles.title: Solid Background Fill
subarticles.summary: Sets the single color behind the whole screen when the background is a solid color. Defaults to white. Match it to your theme and ad creative, and keep it high-contrast against your text and buttons so everything stays easy to read on a phone.

subarticles.title: What Fills The Background
subarticles.summary: Chooses what sits behind your content: a solid color, a photo, or a video clip, and reveals the matching control below. Defaults to a solid color. Use solid for clean question screens, a photo for emotive intro screens, and video only for short high-impact openers, since heavy video slows loading and can lose paid-ad visitors.

subarticles.title: Full-Screen Background Video
subarticles.summary: Uploads a short clip that fills the screen background when the background is set to Video Clip; it loops on its own. Keep it brief and lightweight, large videos slow the first load and can lose paid-ad visitors before they engage. Make sure any text over it stays readable across the looping frames.

subarticles.summary: Screen-level behaviour: entrance animations, cached media, a device-permission prompt, and auto-advance. This guide documents every setting of the Basic Config block, grouped by area. Each setting matches a real control in the screen editor.

subarticles.title: Basic Config section
subarticles.summary: Behavior settings for this screen that do not change its visible copy: the entry animation, preferring cached assets, requesting a system permission, and an optional auto-advance countdown. Most screens can be left at their defaults — reach for these only for timed intros or permission prompts.

subarticles.title: Where it appears
subarticles.summary: Covered screen types: HeroContent, ListMultiPick, ListSinglePick, GridMultiPick, GridSinglePick, TextInput, WheelPicker, HeroList, WebEmbed, Paywall.

subarticles.title: Play Screen Animations
subarticles.summary: Turns on the entrance, exit, and element animations you set up in the screen's animation settings; when off, the screen simply appears instantly. Use it on intro and hero screens where motion feels polished and guides the eye. Leave it off on dense question screens where visitors want the controls ready to tap right away.

subarticles.title: Auto-Advance Duration
subarticles.summary: The number of seconds or minutes (unit chosen below) before the screen moves on by itself, from 1 to 300. Only used when auto-advance is on. Keep it short, about 2 to 4 seconds for a splash or 'analyzing...' screen, so visitors aren't left waiting and bouncing.

subarticles.title: Auto-Advance After A Delay
subarticles.summary: When on, the screen moves to the next step on its own after the countdown you set below, with a visible timer. Off by default. Great for splash or 'analyzing...' screens, but never use it where visitors must tap or answer, like questions or your paywall, or you'll skip them past the response or sale.

subarticles.title: Seconds Or Minutes
subarticles.summary: Sets whether the auto-advance duration above counts in seconds or minutes. Only shows when auto-advance is on. Seconds is the right choice for nearly every onboarding screen; minutes is rarely useful and risks visitors leaving before the screen ever advances.

subarticles.title: Reuse cached media
subarticles.summary: When on, the screen reuses media it has already cached instead of re-downloading it, which can speed up loading for visitors on slow or flaky connections. Leave it off by default for standard web ad funnels, since there's nothing to reuse until assets are cached. Turn it on only if you ship pre-bundled assets or expect a lot of poor-connectivity traffic.

subarticles.title: Which Permission To Ask For
subarticles.summary: Picks which device permission this screen requests: push notifications, ad tracking (needed for accurate ad attribution on iPhones), or location. Only shows when the permission request is turned on. Choose what your funnel truly needs, ad tracking if you rely on ad-network attribution, notifications for re-engaging users later.

subarticles.title: Ask For A Device Permission
subarticles.summary: When on, this screen pops the phone's own permission request, notifications, location, or ad tracking, chosen in the field below, as it appears. This fires in the native app SDK, not on a plain web page. Put it on a screen that first explains why you need it so far more people tap Allow.

subarticles.title: Carousel — every setting
subarticles.summary: An auto-advancing slide deck — the slide template, total play time, each slide’s text and picture and timing, and the per-slide text/image styles. This guide documents every setting of the Carousel block, grouped by area. Each setting matches a real control in the screen editor.

subarticles.title: Carousel section
subarticles.summary: Configures a Carousel screen — a set of slides (image plus optional text) that auto-advance on a timer to tell a quick visual story. Use it for a punchy intro, and keep slides few and fast so visitors reach the next step.

subarticles.title: Where it appears
subarticles.summary: Covered screen types: Carousel.

subarticles.title: Extra line look
subarticles.summary: Open this to override the third line's font size, weight, color, alignment, and the padding around it; it appears only with the Image + Title + 2 Subtitles template. Style it as the smallest, quietest text so it never competes with the headline or supporting line. Leave it on theme defaults unless you truly need a change, since overrides apply to this line on every slide of the carousel.

subarticles.title: Total play time
subarticles.summary: The total time in seconds for the whole carousel to play through once before it stops or the visitor moves on (0.1–120s). This total is split across slides by each slide's timing slider, so changing it speeds up or slows every slide proportionally. Start around 3–5 seconds per slide (about 12–20s for four slides) — long enough to read each line, short enough to keep momentum and avoid stalling the visitor.

subarticles.title: Image box height and position
subarticles.summary: Controls the box that holds each slide's image, separate from the image's own styling. Set how tall the box is (Auto fits the image, Fixed is an exact pixel height, Percent is a share of the slide), where the image sits inside it, and the padding around it. Leave it on Auto unless you want every slide's image to occupy the same vertical space so slides don't jump in size as visitors swipe.

subarticles.title: Image size and fit
subarticles.summary: Open this to control the slide image's width, height, corner radius, and how it fills its box: Fit shows the whole image (may leave bands), Fill covers the box (edges may crop), Crop trims to the exact box, and Tile repeats it. You also set the padding around the image. Fill is the usual choice for full-bleed slides and Fit keeps the whole graphic visible; settings apply to the image on every slide.

subarticles.title: Slide extra line
subarticles.summary: A third text line below the supporting line, available only with the Image + Title + 2 Subtitles template. Use it sparingly for one last small detail like a disclaimer or extra proof, since four text layers over an image quickly overcrowd a slide and slow reading. Supports @variable personalization, countdown timers, and styled chips, and is edited per language.

subarticles.title: How long this slide shows
subarticles.summary: A two-thumb slider that sets the window, as a share of the carousel's total duration, during which this slide is on screen. Drag the thumbs apart to give this slide a longer share, which leaves less time for the others. For example, a 25% window at a 20-second total keeps this slide visible about 5 seconds; keep slides spread evenly and only widen the most persuasive one.

subarticles.title: Slide picture
subarticles.summary: The image shown on this slide, required on every slide no matter which template you pick. Drag-and-drop or click to upload, and Segmently serves a fast-loading optimized version automatically. Use a high-quality picture that matches the slide's message; how it fills the slide is set in Image styles below, and a slide left without an image shows blank, so set one on every slide before publishing.

subarticles.title: Slide supporting line
subarticles.summary: The line under the headline, shown only when the slide template is Image + Title + Subtitle or richer. Use it to back up the headline with a quick proof point or detail rather than repeat it. It supports @variable personalization, countdown timers, and styled chips, is edited per language, and only appears after you set a slide template that includes a subtitle.

subarticles.title: Slide headline
subarticles.summary: The main headline on this slide, shown only when the slide template includes a title. Keep it short and benefit-led so it lands in the few seconds the slide is on screen. You can drop in the visitor's earlier answers with @variable, plus countdown timers and styled label chips; if your funnel runs in several languages, you edit this text per language.

subarticles.title: Slide content template
subarticles.summary: Sets which layers each slide shows: Image Only is just the picture, Image + Title adds one headline, Image + Title + Subtitle adds a supporting line, and Image + Title + 2 Subtitles shows all four text layers. Choosing a richer template reveals its matching text and style fields below. Default to Image + Title for clean, fast-reading slides and add subtitles only when each slide genuinely needs more copy.

subarticles.title: Supporting line look
subarticles.summary: Open this to override the supporting line's font size, weight, color, alignment, and the padding around it; it shows only when the template includes a subtitle. Keep this line visually lighter than the headline (smaller or thinner) so the slide reads in the right order. Leave it on theme defaults for consistency unless this carousel needs a custom look, and remember changes apply to every slide.

subarticles.title: Text box height and position
subarticles.summary: Controls the box that holds all of a slide's text (title, subtitle, detail) as a group, separate from styling each line. Set how tall the box is (Auto fits the text, Fixed is exact pixels, Percent is a share of the slide), where the text block sits, and the padding around it. Leave it on Auto unless you want text anchored the same way on every slide, for example always sitting in the lower third over the image.

subarticles.title: Title look and spacing
subarticles.summary: Open this to override how the carousel's headline looks: font size, weight, color, alignment, and the padding around the text. It only shows when the template includes a title. Leave it untouched to inherit your theme so screens stay consistent; change it only when one carousel needs a bigger or bolder headline, and note the overrides apply to the title on every slide.

subarticles.summary: The Content section holds the words on the screen: your headline, supporting text, or the question you ask the visitor. This is the copy that does the persuading, so write it like ad copy with one clear value proposition or one focused question per screen, and edit it before you touch colors or layout. subarticles.summary: Covered screen types: HeroContent, ListMultiPick, ListSinglePick, GridMultiPick, GridSinglePick, TextInput, WheelPicker, HeroList.

subarticles.title: How rounded the image is
subarticles.summary: Rounds all four corners of the hero image; 0 is sharp and higher values (up to 50) make them softer and more rounded. The default is 0. A small radius around 8 to 16 gives a modern, friendly look; match it to the rounding used elsewhere in your funnel, like buttons and cards, so the page feels consistent.

subarticles.title: Size the image by screen
subarticles.summary: Sizes the hero image as a percentage of the screen height (0 to 100%), so it scales with the device, the more responsive way to size a hero. If set, it overrides any fixed height above. A common starting point is 30 to 50% for a prominent banner that still leaves room for your title and button below; leave it empty to size by proportions instead.

subarticles.title: Fixed image height
subarticles.summary: Optionally pin the hero image to a set height with the slider (0–500) or by typing a number. Leave it empty to let the image keep its natural proportions from the width — best for most screens. Use a fixed height when you want a consistent banner size; to size by screen proportion instead, use 'Image height relative to container' below, which takes priority over this value.

subarticles.title: Space around the image
subarticles.summary: Adds empty space on each side of the hero image (top, right, bottom, left) so it isn't flush against the screen edges or crammed next to the title. Leave it at the theme default in most cases. Increase a side when the image feels too tight against nearby content, or reduce it for a full-bleed, edge-to-edge look.

subarticles.title: How the image fills its box
subarticles.summary: Sets how your image fits its box: Aspect Fit shows the whole image with no cropping (you may see empty bars at the sides), Aspect Fill crops the edges so it fully covers the box, Scale to Fill stretches it (can look distorted, avoid for photos), and Tile repeats it as a pattern. Default is Aspect Fit, which never distorts; switch to Aspect Fill when you want it edge-to-edge and don't mind some cropping.

subarticles.title: The hero image itself
subarticles.summary: Pick the actual hero image: upload a file from your computer or paste a direct image URL, then check the preview thumbnail. Use a high-resolution JPG or PNG so it stays crisp on large screens — uploads are optimized automatically for fast loading. To change it later, just upload or paste a new source here.

subarticles.title: Fixed image width
subarticles.summary: Optionally pin the hero image to a set width with the slider (0–500) or by typing a number. Leave it empty in most cases — the image then sizes to the screen and stays responsive across devices, which almost always looks best on a landing page. Set a fixed width only when you need the image smaller than full-width or aligned to a specific size.

subarticles.title: The featured image up top
subarticles.summary: The hero is the large featured image at the top of a headline or wheel-picker screen, the picture that sells the screen at a glance. Turn it on, then upload a file or paste an image URL. Pick a high-quality, on-message visual (product, result, or lifestyle shot); on a paid landing page it is often the first thing a visitor sees. Sizing and position are set just below.

subarticles.title: Where the image sits
subarticles.summary: On headline screens, this sets where the hero image sits relative to your title and subtitle — above the text, below it, or beside it. Lead with your strongest element: image-on-top when the visual is the hook, text-on-top when the headline does the selling. The preview updates instantly, so try a couple and keep whichever reads clearest.

subarticles.title: Space around the subtitle
subarticles.summary: Adds empty space on each side of the subtitle, controlling the gap above it (to the title) and below it (to what follows). Leave it at the theme default unless the subtitle feels crowded. Increase the top value to separate it from the title, or reduce spacing to tighten the whole headline group.

subarticles.title: Subtitle look and emphasis
subarticles.summary: Change how the subtitle looks — font, size, weight, color, alignment, and an optional background — styled separately from the title so you can tune each one. By default it inherits your theme (usually smaller and lighter than the title), which works for most funnels. Override only when a specific screen needs different emphasis.

subarticles.title: Write the subtitle text
subarticles.summary: Type the supporting line that sits under your title here, one short sentence that reinforces the offer or tells the visitor what comes next. The same shortcuts work as in the title: type @ to insert an earlier answer, @link to add a clickable link, or @countdown for urgency. If your funnel is multilingual, text is saved per language, so switch language before editing each translation.

subarticles.title: The line under your title
subarticles.summary: The subtitle is the supporting line beneath your title; use it to expand the promise, add proof, or hint at what happens next. Turn it on and keep it to one short sentence; it shows smaller and lighter than the title by default so the headline stays dominant. Like the title, you can personalize it with @ variables. Skip it on screens where the title already says everything.

subarticles.title: Space around the title
subarticles.summary: Adds empty space on each side of the title (top, right, bottom, left) so it isn't cramped against the screen edges or the text below. Leave it at the theme default unless the title feels too tight or too far from the next element. Increase a side to give it room, or decrease to pull elements closer together.

subarticles.title: Title look and emphasis
subarticles.summary: Override how the headline looks — font, size, weight, color, alignment, and an optional highlight behind the text. By default it inherits your project theme, which keeps every screen consistent, so most funnels never need to touch this. Override only when one screen needs extra punch, like a bigger color headline on your hero.

subarticles.title: Write the headline text
subarticles.summary: This is where you type the actual headline; keep it short and benefit-driven. Type @ to pull in a visitor's earlier answer (such as @user_goal) for personalization, add a link inside the text with @link, or insert a countdown with @countdown to create urgency on offer screens. If your funnel runs in more than one language, text is saved per language, so switch language before editing each translation.

Type @ to drop in an earlier answer (for example @user_goal) so it feels personal, and style it under the gear icon below.

articles.oneLineSummary: Documents the Custom HTML or WebEmbed section for embedding custom iframe or HTML experiences inside a Segmently screen. It covers the code editor, Apply to Preview, iframe isolation and sandbox settings, external data sources, and boundaries between WebEmbed paywalls, analytics scripts, and custom domain setup.

subarticles.title: All settings
subarticles.summary: All settings

subarticles.title: Custom HTML — every setting
subarticles.summary: The Custom HTML settings for this screen. This guide documents every setting of the Custom HTML block, grouped by area. Each setting matches a real control in the screen editor.

subarticles.title: Custom HTML section
subarticles.summary: The Custom HTML section lets you render your own HTML, CSS, and JavaScript inside a screen when none of the built-in sections fit the design you need. The content runs in an isolated frame and connects to the funnel so it can read data and trigger navigation. Reach for it only for fully custom screens like a Figma export or a bespoke widget — for standard text, buttons, lists, or paywalls use the native sections, which stay responsive and tracked, and always preview custom screens on a phone.

subarticles.title: Where it appears
subarticles.summary: Covered screen types: WebEmbed.

subarticles.title: Editable content for your HTML
subarticles.summary: Adds reusable pieces of content (text, images, and more) that your custom HTML can read by name, so copy and visuals live in the editor instead of being hard-coded. In code you fetch one by its name, which lets you or a non-developer update content later without touching the HTML. The Image URL Scanner can auto-create media sources from external image links it finds, so those images get hosted and tracked by Segmently.

subarticles.title: Your custom screen code
subarticles.summary: Write the HTML, CSS, and JavaScript that renders inside this custom screen here. Edits stay local until you click Apply to Preview, then they appear in the preview. Critically, your code must call segmentlySDK.navigateNext to advance the funnel and segmentlySDK.getChildSection to read any data sources you've added — without navigateNext, visitors get stuck and never reach your paywall.

subarticles.title: Keep custom code sandboxed
subarticles.summary: Decides whether your custom HTML runs in a protected sandbox (On, the default) or directly in the page (Off). Leave it On — the sandbox stops your CSS and JavaScript from leaking out and breaking the rest of the screen. Only switch it Off if your code truly needs to reach the surrounding page, and expect to debug styling clashes if you do.

subarticles.summary: Each section type has its own guide

subarticles.title: Embedded block links
subarticles.summary: A section’s own content and styling — Text, Media, Buttons, Options, Product Catalog and the rest — are documented once in their own articles and reused everywhere they appear, so nothing is duplicated. Links to each of those guides will be added here. The rest of this article covers only what is specific to a Flexible Layout screen: managing sections, their per-section layout, the whole-screen layout, and the sticky bar.

subarticles.title: Composition intro
subarticles.summary: A Flexible Layout screen is one you build yourself: you add sections — text, media, a product catalog, buttons, lists and more — then stack, size and align them however you like. The settings below cover what is unique to assembling the screen; each section type’s own content and styling lives in its own guide (see the note at the end).

subarticles.title: Link product-aware sections
subarticles.summary: Some Flexible Layout sections can read the visitor’s current Product Catalog selection. For a paywall, add a Product Catalog section, then link a Text section and a Purchase Button section to that catalog through each section’s “Linked to section” dropdown. The linked Text section can show the selected product description label, and the linked Purchase Button can show the selected product purchase label.

If you leave the Purchase Button label empty, it falls back to the product’s purchase label. When the button is linked to the catalog, tapping it purchases the selected product, not a fixed default product.

subarticles.title: Flexible Sections — every setting
subarticles.summary: The build-your-own screen — you stack sections (text, media, product catalog, buttons, lists…) and arrange them: add / reorder / rename / delete, set each section’s size, fill, alignment, border, padding and margin, control whole-screen scroll and padding, and link product-aware sections (for example Text or Purchase Button) to a Product Catalog so labels and purchases follow the selected product. Each section type’s own content and styling lives in its dedicated block article. This guide documents every setting of the Flexible Sections block, grouped by area. Each setting matches a real control in the screen editor.

subarticles.title: Flexible Sections section
subarticles.summary: Builds a FlexibleLayout screen from stacked sections you arrange yourself, giving full control over the vertical order, sizing, and spacing of pieces (media, text, buttons). Use it when the standard screen types do not give you the layout you need.

subarticles.title: Where it appears
subarticles.summary: Covered screen types: FlexibleLayout.

subarticles.title: Add a new section
subarticles.summary: Use + Add to choose what kind of block to place on this FlexibleLayout screen: text, media, product catalog, button, purchase button, list, custom embed, text field, spacer, header, footer, or paywall header. Add sections in the same order a visitor should read them, then drag to reorder if the screen flow changes. Start with the biggest structure first — for example header, hero text/media, products, and CTA — then tune layout settings inside each section.

subarticles.title: Background fill color
subarticles.summary: Sets the color behind this section's content, used when the background type is Solid. The default is white. Enter a hex code or pick a swatch, and keep it in line with your theme so the screen feels on-brand, with enough contrast against the text on top to stay readable.

subarticles.title: Solid color or image behind
subarticles.summary: Sets what fills the area behind this section's content. Solid (the default) uses one color you pick below; Media places an image behind the content for a richer, ad-style look. If you go with Media and put text on top, keep the text readable with a darker image or an overlay so your value proposition doesn't get lost.

subarticles.title: Outline color
subarticles.summary: Sets the color of the section's outline. The default is black, and it only shows when the border thickness is above 0, so set a width first. Match it to one of your theme's accent colors for a clean, on-brand frame around the section.

subarticles.title: Outline thickness
subarticles.summary: Draws an outline around the section. The default 0 means no border; 1 to 2 pixels gives a subtle frame that makes a section read as a self-contained card or highlights an offer. Set this above 0 first, then pick the border color below.

subarticles.title: Set button color
subarticles.summary: Hex color for button background. Default yellow-gold (#ffc201). Primary visual element for call-to-action buttons.

subarticles.title: Set button border color
subarticles.summary: Hex color for button border line. Only visible when border width is greater than 0.

subarticles.title: Set button border thickness
subarticles.summary: Button border stroke width in pixels (0-50). Default 0 (no border). Used with border color for outlined button style.

subarticles.title: Round button corners
subarticles.summary: Uniform corner radius (0-50 pixels) for all button corners. Default 12 creates slightly rounded button. Higher values create pill-shaped buttons.

subarticles.title: Button visual effects
subarticles.summary: Optional finishing touches for the button, such as overall transparency and entrance or tap animations. Use a subtle animation to draw the eye to a primary call-to-action, or lower the transparency to play down a secondary button. Leave it off for a plain, static button.

subarticles.title: Gradient color fill
subarticles.summary: Optional. Layers a color gradient over the button's solid background for a richer, more premium look. Pick Simple (two colors), Medium (two colors plus a tilt angle), or Advanced (several color stops, with optional shimmer). Leave it off if a flat color is enough; turn it on to make a primary button catch the eye.

subarticles.title: Optional icon on the button
subarticles.summary: Adds a small image beside the button label, positioned left or right of the text, with controls for its size and surrounding spacing. Use a simple icon to reinforce the action — like an arrow on a 'Continue' button — and upload a transparent PNG or SVG so it sits cleanly. Leave it empty for a clean text-only button.

subarticles.title: Inner spacing around the label
subarticles.summary: Sets the breathing room between the label or icon and the button's edges, set separately for top, bottom, left, and right. More padding makes the button bigger and easier to tap; too little makes it look cramped. Generous top and bottom padding gives a primary button a comfortable, finger-friendly tap area.

subarticles.title: Drop shadow under the button
subarticles.summary: Optional. Casts a soft shadow beneath the button so it appears lifted off the screen, which helps a primary action stand out. Adjust blur for softness, spread for size, opacity for strength, and offset for direction. A subtle shadow usually looks best; leave it off for a flat, minimal style.

subarticles.title: Align button text
subarticles.summary: Text alignment within button: start (left in LTR), center, or end (right in LTR). Center alignment is typical for buttons.

subarticles.title: Set button text color
subarticles.summary: Hex color for button label text. Default black (#000000). Must contrast with button background for readability.

subarticles.title: Font for the button text
subarticles.summary: Picks the typeface used for the button label. Leave it on your theme default so the button matches the rest of your funnel — mixing fonts on one screen looks unpolished and can hurt trust. Only override it when your brand requires a specific font.

subarticles.title: Size of the button label
subarticles.summary: Sets how large the text on the button appears. Most buttons read well at 16-18; go larger to make a primary action more prominent, but watch that the label doesn't wrap or overflow on small phone screens. Keep it consistent across your buttons so the screen looks intentional.

subarticles.title: Boldness of the label
subarticles.summary: Sets how thick the button text is, from 400 (regular) through 700 (bold) and beyond. Bolder text draws the eye, so use 600-700 for a primary action you want people to tap. Keep lighter weights for secondary or less important buttons.

subarticles.title: Spacing between wrapped lines
subarticles.summary: Sets the vertical gap between lines when a button label is long enough to wrap onto two or more lines. Most buttons use a single short label, so the default is fine and you can ignore this. Nudge it up only if a multi-line button looks cramped or hard to read.

subarticles.title: Wording on the button
subarticles.summary: The text shown on the button (placeholder 'Button Text'). Use a short, action-led phrase like 'Continue', 'Get Started', or 'Next' so people know exactly what tapping does. If your funnel runs in more than one language, this wording is saved per language, so set it for each one you support.

subarticles.title: Space around the whole section stack
subarticles.summary: Container padding adds space between the phone edges and all sections on the screen. It is different from Section padding: container padding moves the entire stack inward, while section padding adds space inside one selected section. Use container padding first when every block feels too close to the screen edge, then use per-section padding only where a specific block needs more breathing room.

subarticles.title: Round the section corners
subarticles.summary: Rounds all four corners of the section. The default 0 keeps them sharp and square; higher values (try 8 to 16) give a soft card look that pairs well with a solid background or border to make the section stand out as its own block. The range is 0 to 50 pixels.

subarticles.title: Delete a section
subarticles.summary: Use the trash icon to remove a section from the screen. Deleting also removes that section's content and can affect buttons linked to it, so confirm only after checking the preview and any parent-section links. If you are unsure, rename the section first or move it lower in the order while you verify the layout instead of deleting it immediately.

subarticles.title: Stretch to fill empty space
subarticles.summary: Controls how much leftover vertical space a section soaks up so the screen has no awkward gap. 0 keeps a section at its natural size (the default for text and buttons); 1 or more lets it stretch, and a section set to 2 takes twice the extra space as one set to 1. Raise this on your image or hero section to push the button down to a comfortable spot. Only applies when the section isn't set to scroll.

subarticles.title: Let it shrink on small screens
subarticles.summary: Controls which section gives up height first when everything can't fit on a small phone. Higher numbers shrink sooner; 0 means never shrink this one. The default of 1 lets sections shrink evenly. Set 0 on must-stay pieces like the button or logo, and raise it on a less important section like a tall image, so the key content survives intact on the smallest screens.

subarticles.title: How tall this section is
subarticles.summary: Decides how the section's height is calculated. Auto (the safe default) makes it exactly as tall as its content, which is right for most text and buttons. Fixed lets you type an exact pixel height, and Percent sets it to a share of the screen, handy for a hero image that should always fill, say, the top 40 percent. Your pick also decides which value box below applies.

subarticles.title: The height number
subarticles.summary: This is the number that pairs with your height mode. With Fixed mode, type pixels (0 to 1000, for example 320 for a tall hero); with Percent mode, type a share of the screen (0 to 100, for example 40). The box is ignored in Auto mode. For a scrollable section, this also sets the visible window the content scrolls inside.

subarticles.title: Left, center, or right
subarticles.summary: Positions the content along the section's width: Left, Center, or Right. Center is the usual choice for headlines and buttons, while Left reads more naturally for longer body copy. (Left and right follow text direction, so they flip on right-to-left languages.)

subarticles.title: Link the Purchase Button to the same catalog
subarticles.summary: Use the Purchase Button’s “Linked to section” dropdown to select the same Product Catalog section. This keeps the CTA tied to the visitor’s selected plan instead of a fixed product.

subarticles.title: Link product-aware sections
subarticles.summary: Some Flexible Layout sections can read the visitor’s current Product Catalog selection. For a paywall, add a Product Catalog section, then link a Text section and a Purchase Button section to that catalog through each section’s “Linked to section” dropdown. The linked Text section can show the selected product description label, and the linked Purchase Button can show the selected product purchase label.

subarticles.title: Space between sections
subarticles.summary: Margin is the gap outside a section, between it and the sections next to it. Set Top, Bottom, Left, and Right independently, using positive values to push sections apart. A negative top margin pulls a section up so it overlaps the one above — for example, a headline resting on a hero image; pair that with stacking order to control what sits in front.

subarticles.title: Text below or over the image
subarticles.summary: Decides whether your text and buttons sit below the image or float on top of it. Below media keeps content in its own space under the image — the safest choice for readability. Overlapping media lets the headline drift over the lower part of the image for a magazine-style hero; if you use it, add an overlay or gradient so the text stays legible against the picture.

subarticles.title: Round the image corners
subarticles.summary: Rounds the corners of the image or video. The default 0 is square; try 8 to 16 for a soft, modern look or a higher value for a strongly rounded card. Match it to the rounding on nearby buttons and sections so the whole screen feels cohesive.

subarticles.title: Dark fade for readable text
subarticles.summary: Adds a dark fade over the bottom of the image or video so text placed on top stays readable. It's strongest at the bottom and clears toward the top. The default is black, which is the usual choice (or a dark brand color). Use it whenever you let content overlap the media so your headline and button don't get lost in a busy image.

subarticles.title: How much height the image takes
subarticles.summary: Sets how much of the section's height the image or video fills, as a percentage. The default 50 splits the space evenly and leaves the lower half for your headline and button. Raise it (around 70) for a bold, image-led screen, or lower it when you need more room for copy and a clear call to action.

subarticles.title: Loop the video
subarticles.summary: For video media only: turn on to loop the clip continuously, or leave off to play it once and stop. Looping suits short, ambient hero or background videos that keep the screen feeling alive, while play-once suits a clip with a clear start and finish. It has no effect on still images.

subarticles.title: How the image fills its area
subarticles.summary: Decides how your image or video fits the section. Fill covers the whole area and crops the edges that don't fit — best for full-bleed hero shots and the right pick for most ad creatives. Fit shows the entire image but may leave blank bars around it; use it when nothing can be cropped. Stretch forces an exact fit but distorts the picture, so avoid it for photos.

subarticles.title: Where the image starts on screen
subarticles.summary: Sets the top edge of your image or video. Screen Top runs it all the way up behind the status bar and header for a full-bleed, edge-to-edge hero. Header Bottom starts it just below the header bar so a back button or progress bar stays clearly visible. Pick Screen Top for an immersive opener, Header Bottom when the header needs to read cleanly.

subarticles.title: Open one section's settings
subarticles.summary: Click the gear inside a section card to open that section's own settings. The first panel controls the section container — height, flex, scrollability, background, borders, alignment, padding, and margin — and the panel below controls the section's content, such as text, media, products, or button styling. This is the main place to tune how one block looks and behaves.

subarticles.title: Breathing room inside the section
subarticles.summary: Padding is the space inside a section, between its edges and the content sitting in it. Set Top, Bottom, Left, and Right independently, starting from 0. Add some so text and buttons don't crowd the section border or a background image; 16-24 px all around is a comfortable, readable starting point.

subarticles.title: Set purchase button color
subarticles.summary: Hex color for purchase button background. Default yellow-gold (#ffc201). Distinguishes purchase action from regular navigation.

subarticles.title: Purchase button border color
subarticles.summary: Sets the color of the outline around the purchase button. It only shows up when the border thickness is above 0, so set a thickness first. Use it to give an outlined-style call-to-action a clean, contrasting edge.

subarticles.title: Purchase button border thickness
subarticles.summary: Sets how thick the outline around the purchase button is, from 0 to 50 pixels. The default is 0, meaning no border; set a value together with a border color to create an outlined button. A solid filled button usually converts better, so most paywalls leave this at 0.

subarticles.title: Roundness of the button corners
subarticles.summary: Rounds all four corners of the purchase button by the same amount, from sharp to fully rounded (0-50). The default of about 12 gives a softly rounded look; raise it toward 50 for a pill-shaped button, or set 0 for crisp square corners. Match it to your other buttons so the paywall feels cohesive.

subarticles.title: Offer a cheaper plan on cancel
subarticles.summary: Controls what happens when someone cancels the payment. When on, they're sent to a downsale screen offering a cheaper or alternative plan — a second chance to recover the sale. When off, cancelling just sends them back with no further offer. Only turn this on if you've actually built a downsale screen in the funnel, otherwise there's nothing for it to open.

subarticles.title: Purchase button effects
subarticles.summary: Optional finishing touches for the purchase button, such as overall transparency and entrance or tap animations. A subtle pulse or scale animation can pull attention to your call-to-action and lift conversions. Leave it off for a static button.

subarticles.title: Purchase button gradient
subarticles.summary: Optionally lays a color gradient over the button's solid background for a richer call-to-action. Pick Simple (two colors), Medium (two colors plus an angle), or Advanced (multiple color stops, with an optional shimmer). Use it to make your main CTA pop; leave it off if a flat color already stands out.

subarticles.title: Purchase button icon
subarticles.summary: Optionally shows a small image next to the button label, to the left or right of the text. Upload an icon, then set its size and the spacing around it. A lock or arrow icon can reinforce the action, but a clean text-only button works just as well.

subarticles.title: Inner spacing around the label
subarticles.summary: Sets the breathing room between the label or icon and the purchase button's edges, set separately for top, bottom, left, and right. More padding makes the button taller and easier to tap; too little looks cramped. Generous top and bottom padding helps your main purchase button feel substantial and inviting to press.

subarticles.title: Purchase button shadow
subarticles.summary: Optionally adds a soft shadow beneath the button so it lifts off the screen and pulls the eye toward your call-to-action. You can tune the softness (blur), size (spread), strength (opacity), and direction (offset). A subtle shadow usually works best; leave it off for a flat design.

subarticles.title: Purchase button text alignment
subarticles.summary: Sets where the label sits inside the button: start (left in left-to-right languages), center, or end (right). Center is the standard choice and is recommended for a call-to-action so the label reads as one clear, balanced action.

subarticles.title: Purchase button text color
subarticles.summary: Sets the color of the words on your purchase button. Make sure it contrasts strongly with the button background so the label stays easy to read — for example, dark text on the default yellow-gold button. Weak contrast means users miss the action, which directly costs you conversions.

subarticles.title: Purchase button font
subarticles.summary: Picks the typeface for the purchase button label, such as SF Pro or Helvetica. Match it to the rest of your paywall so the call-to-action looks intentional rather than out of place. Leave it on the theme default unless your brand uses a specific font.

subarticles.title: Purchase button text size
subarticles.summary: Sets how big the label on your purchase button looks, measured in points. Since this is your main paywall call-to-action, keep it large and unmistakable — around 17 to 20 pt works well on most screens. Avoid going so big that the text wraps or spills outside the button on smaller phones.

subarticles.title: Purchase button text weight
subarticles.summary: Controls how thick or bold the button label appears, on a scale from 400 (regular) to 700 (bold) and heavier. As your primary call-to-action it should look bold and confident — a weight of 600 to 700 helps it visually dominate any secondary buttons on the screen.

subarticles.title: Purchase button line spacing
subarticles.summary: Controls the vertical gap between lines when the button label runs onto two or more lines. Most call-to-action labels fit on one line, so you can leave this on the default. Adjust it only if a longer label looks cramped or too loose when it wraps.

subarticles.title: Wording on the buy button
subarticles.summary: The text on your paywall's purchase button (default 'Subscribe Now'). This is the most important call to action in the whole funnel, so make it clear and benefit-led, such as 'Start My Free Trial' or 'Unlock Full Access'. If you run multiple languages, this wording is saved per language, so translate it for each.

subarticles.title: Reorder sections
subarticles.summary: Drag the handle beside a section name to change the vertical reading order on the screen. The order here is the order visitors see in the preview and published flow, so keep the persuasion sequence clear: context first, offer/details next, then the CTA. After reordering, recheck fixed-height and flex settings because a section that worked in one position may need different spacing in another.

subarticles.title: Let the whole screen scroll
subarticles.summary: When Scrollable screen is on, sections stack vertically and the visitor can scroll through them. Use this for long paywalls, product catalogs, benefit lists, or any screen with more content than fits on a phone. When it is off, the screen uses flexGrow and flexShrink to distribute sections inside one viewport, which is better for fixed hero layouts where the CTA should stay visible without scrolling.

subarticles.title: Open screen-level layout settings
subarticles.summary: The gear beside the Sections title opens settings for the whole FlexibleLayout screen, not for one individual section. Use it to control whether the full screen scrolls and how much padding the whole stack has from the screen edges. Open this before editing individual section padding when the entire screen feels too close to the phone edge or when you need a fixed, non-scrolling composition.

subarticles.title: Let this section scroll on its own
subarticles.summary: Turn on to let a section scroll independently when its content is taller than the height you set (works only with a Fixed or Percent height, not Auto). Use it for a long list of terms or bullets you want capped inside a fixed window while the rest of the screen stays put. Leave off (the default) for normal sections that just sit in the layout.

subarticles.title: Rename a section for editing
subarticles.summary: Click the pencil beside a section name to give it a clear internal label, such as Hero headline, Annual plan list, or Bottom CTA. This name helps editors understand the structure and is not shown to visitors. Rename repeated sections immediately so it is obvious which block you are opening, especially when several Text or Button sections exist on the same screen.

subarticles.title: Selected product drives labels and purchase
subarticles.summary: When the visitor changes the selected plan, linked labels update from that selected product. If you leave the Text title empty, it falls back to the product’s description label. If you leave the Purchase Button label empty, it falls back to the product’s purchase label. When the button is linked to the catalog, tapping it purchases the selected product, not a fixed default product.

subarticles.title: Verify checkout uses the selected product
subarticles.summary: For paid-trial, no-trial, and one-time products, verify a payment_intent with non-empty amount and currency. For free-trial subscriptions, verify setup_intent. This proves the linked purchase button buys the currently selected product.

subarticles.title: Updated selected product labels
subarticles.summary: After selecting a different Product Catalog item, the linked Text label and Purchase Button label update to that product’s description and purchase labels.

subarticles.title: Left, center, or right text
subarticles.summary: Sets whether the text reads from the Left, Center, or Right. Center suits short headlines and call-to-action lines, while Left is easier to read for longer body copy. (Left and right follow language direction and flip on right-to-left locales.)

subarticles.title: Text color
subarticles.summary: Sets the color of this text. The default is black. Always check it against the section background: dark text on light backgrounds, and light or white text over dark or image backgrounds. Low-contrast text is hard to read and a common reason visitors bounce, so keep your message legible.

subarticles.title: Pick the font
subarticles.summary: Sets which typeface this text uses. By default it follows your theme font, which keeps the whole funnel looking consistent, so change it only for a deliberate accent. Stick to one or two fonts across the funnel so it reads as polished and on-brand to paid visitors.

subarticles.title: Text size
subarticles.summary: Sets the font size in points, where bigger means more prominent. As a guide, about 24 to 40 works for a headline and 14 to 18 for body copy, keeping a clear hierarchy. This overrides your theme's default size for this text, so change it only when this section needs to stand apart from the rest.

subarticles.title: How heavy the text looks
subarticles.summary: Controls how thick the text appears. Common picks are 400 for regular body copy, 600 for semibold, and 700 for bold headlines and call-to-action lines. Put the heaviest weight on the one line you most want visitors to notice and keep body text lighter, so the screen has an easy-to-read hierarchy.

subarticles.title: Spacing between lines
subarticles.summary: Controls the vertical gap between lines in a multi-line block. Roughly 1.3 to 1.5 times the font size reads comfortably for body copy, with tighter spacing for big headlines. Bump it up if a paragraph feels cramped, or down if a headline's lines drift apart. It only matters when text wraps to more than one line.

subarticles.title: The words in this section
subarticles.summary: Sets the headline or body text shown here. You can drop in dynamic values by typing @ to pick a flow variable, so the screen can echo the visitor's earlier answer, show a label, or run a live countdown, which makes the funnel feel personal and converts better. If your funnel runs in more than one language, this text can be translated per language.

subarticles.title: Top, center, or bottom
subarticles.summary: Pins the content to the Top, Center, or Bottom of the section. It only changes anything when the section is taller than its content, for example with a Fixed or Percent height or a section stretched to fill space. Use Center to vertically center a headline in a tall hero, or Bottom to push a caption to the base of an image.

subarticles.title: Which section sits in front
subarticles.summary: When two sections overlap, this decides which one shows on top. A higher number wins; the default 0 is fine as long as nothing overlaps. You only need it when you've deliberately layered sections, like a headline placed over a background image, so give the part you want visible the higher number.

subarticles.summary: Flexible Sections in the editor

subarticles.title: Context caption
subarticles.summary: Open the Flexible Sections section in the screen editor to configure its settings.

subarticles.title: Space around the whole section stack
subarticles.summary: Container padding adds space between the phone edges and all sections on the screen. It is different from Section padding: container padding moves the entire stack inward, while section padding adds space inside one selected section. Use container padding first when every block feels too close to the screen edge, then use per-section padding only where a specific block needs more breathing room.

When it is off, the screen uses flexGrow and flexShrink to distribute sections inside one viewport, which is better for fixed hero layouts where the CTA should stay visible without scrolling.

subarticles.title: Solid color or image behind

If you go with Media and put text on top, keep the text readable with a darker image or an overlay so your value proposition doesn't get lost.

subarticles.title: Outline color
subarticles.summary: Sets the color of the section's outline. The default is black, and it only shows when the border thickness is above 0, so set a width first. Match it to one of your theme's accent colors for a clean, on-brand frame around the section.

subarticles.title: Outline thickness
subarticles.summary: Draws an outline around the section. The default 0 means no border; 1 to 2 pixels gives a subtle frame that makes a section read as a self-contained card or highlights an offer. Set this above 0 first, then pick the border color below.

subarticles.title: Round the section corners
subarticles.summary: Rounds all four corners of the section. The default 0 keeps them sharp and square; higher values (try 8 to 16) give a soft card look that pairs well with a solid background or border to make the section stand out as its own block. The range is 0 to 50 pixels.

subarticles.title: Stretch to fill empty space
subarticles.summary: Controls how much leftover vertical space a section soaks up so the screen has no awkward gap. 0 keeps a section at its natural size (the default for text and buttons); 1 or more lets it stretch, and a section set to 2 takes twice the extra space as one set to 1. Raise this on your image or hero section to push the button down to a comfortable spot. Only applies when the section isn't set to scroll.

subarticles.title: Let it shrink on small screens
subarticles.summary: Controls which section gives up height first when everything can't fit on a small phone. Higher numbers shrink sooner; 0 means never shrink this one. The default of 1 lets sections shrink evenly. Set 0 on must-stay pieces like the button or logo, and raise it on a less important section like a tall image, so the key content survives intact on the smallest screens.

subarticles.title: How tall this section is
subarticles.summary: Decides how the section's height is calculated. Auto (the safe default) makes it exactly as tall as its content, which is right for most text and buttons. Fixed lets you type an exact pixel height, and Percent sets it to a share of the screen, handy for a hero image that should always fill, say, the top 40 percent. For a scrollable section, this also sets the visible window the content scrolls inside.
