subarticles.title: Header — every setting
subarticles.summary: The top bar of the screen — the Back and Skip buttons and the progress indicator that shows how far along the visitor is. This guide documents every setting of the Header block, grouped by area. Each setting matches a real control in the screen editor.

subarticles.title: Header section
subarticles.summary: Controls the bar at the top of the screen: the Back and Skip buttons and the progress indicator that shows how far through the flow a visitor is. Most screens inherit sensible defaults — style the progress indicator (kind and colors) so it matches your brand.

subarticles.title: Where it appears
subarticles.summary: Covered screen types: HeroContent, Carousel, ListMultiPick, ListSinglePick, GridMultiPick, GridSinglePick, ProgressSteps, TextInput, WheelPicker, HeroList, WebEmbed.

subarticles.title: Header Bar Background
subarticles.summary: Fills the header bar with a color, or clear it to transparent so the screen background shows through for a floating header. Use a solid color to set the header apart from busy content. If you go transparent over a photo or video, check that the Back, Skip, and progress colors still stand out clearly.

subarticles.title: Header Bar Height
subarticles.summary: Sets how tall the header bar is, from 20 to 200 pixels, with a default of 44, which is the space its buttons and progress bar share. Keep it near the default for a standard bar and raise it only if you add a tall icon or larger text. Going too small cramps the Back and Skip buttons and makes them hard to tap.

subarticles.title: Header See-Through Level
subarticles.summary: Fades the whole header bar from fully solid to fully see-through, defaulting to solid. Lower it for a soft, partly transparent header that blends into a photo or video background. Keep it high enough that the Back, Skip, and progress controls stay easy to see.

subarticles.title: Back Button Label
subarticles.summary: Sets the text and styling of the Back control that returns visitors to the previous step. Defaults to a left arrow and supports other languages. Keep it small so it doesn't compete with your main action, and clear it to hide the button on the first screen, where there's nowhere to go back to.

subarticles.title: Back button text style
subarticles.summary: Overrides how the Back control's label looks — font, size, weight, color, alignment, line height, an optional highlight behind the text, and a strikethrough color. By default it inherits your project theme, which keeps every screen consistent. Touch this only when the Back label needs to match a specific header treatment, and keep it subtle so it never competes with your main action.

subarticles.title: Spacing inside the header
subarticles.summary: Sets the inner spacing on each side (top, right, bottom, left) that pushes the Back button, Skip button, and progress bar away from the header edges. Raise the top value to keep these controls clear of the phone's status bar or notch, and adjust left/right so buttons aren't jammed against the screen edge. Start from the defaults and nudge only where something looks cramped, since a clean header keeps the first impression of your ad landing page tidy.

subarticles.title: Completed Progress Color
subarticles.summary: Colors the filled, completed part of the progress bar. Defaults to gold for the Line style and teal for Dashes. Use your brand accent and make sure it clearly stands out against the unfilled track color so visitors can see at a glance how far they've come.

subarticles.title: Progress Content Side
subarticles.summary: Sets where the icon and label sit across the header, on the left (Start), centered, or on the right (End). Mostly a cosmetic touch: centered usually looks balanced, while left or right lets you line the label up with your Back or Skip button. Adjust only if the default looks off.

subarticles.title: Stretch Progress Edge-To-Edge
subarticles.summary: When on, the progress bar stretches all the way across the header; when off, it takes only the width its content needs. Use full width for a bold, obvious progress bar across the top of the screen. Turn it off when you want the bar compact and grouped with a label or icon.

subarticles.title: Header icon settings
subarticles.summary: Controls the optional header icon shown next to the progress bar — its image (upload or URL), placement relative to the label, scale mode, width, height, corner rounding, and padding. Off by default. Turn it on only to reinforce branding in the header, and keep the icon small so it doesn't crowd the progress bar or the Back and Skip buttons.

subarticles.title: Optional Header Icon
subarticles.summary: Adds an optional small icon, often a logo or step glyph, next to the progress bar, with controls for the image, its size, and its spacing. Most funnels leave this off. Use it only to reinforce branding in the header, and keep the icon small so it doesn't crowd the progress bar.

subarticles.title: Progress Bar Style
subarticles.summary: Chooses how progress through the funnel looks: a single continuous bar (Line) or segmented dots (Dashes), each with its own color controls below. A visible 'how far along' cue reassures visitors only a few steps remain, which lifts completion. Pick whichever fits your brand and keep it the same across screens.

subarticles.title: Spacing around the progress bar
subarticles.summary: Sets the spacing on each side of the progress indicator alone, separate from the header's overall padding. Use it to fine-tune the gap around the bar, for example to nudge it down from the buttons, without moving the buttons themselves. Most funnels keep the default; adjust only when the bar sits too tight or too loose against the header.

subarticles.title: Keep Progress Clear Of Buttons
subarticles.summary: When on, which is the default, the progress bar shrinks so it never overlaps the Back or Skip buttons; when off, it can collide with them in a tight header. Leave it on. Turn it off only if you've removed those buttons and want the bar to use the full width.

subarticles.title: Progress text style
subarticles.summary: Overrides how the progress label (for example 'Step 5 of 10') looks — font, size, weight, color, alignment, line height, an optional highlight, and a strikethrough color. By default it inherits your theme. Use it to make the reassurance text legible against your header background, and keep it small so it supports rather than overshadows the progress bar.

subarticles.title: Progress Bar Text
subarticles.summary: Optional text shown with the progress bar, such as a 'Step 5 of 10' counter or a short line of reassurance. Supports other languages and styling; leave it empty for a clean bar-only look. Note this text is fixed per screen and won't count up on its own, so use it as a label unless you drive it from a variable.

subarticles.title: Remaining Progress Color
subarticles.summary: Colors the empty, not-yet-completed part of the progress bar. Defaults to white for the Line style and light gray for Dashes. Keep it muted next to the filled color so the completed portion clearly reads as progress rather than blending in.

subarticles.title: Progress Height In Header
subarticles.summary: Sets where the progress bar sits up and down within the header: at the top, centered, or at the bottom. Centered is the usual balanced choice; use bottom to sit it just above your content, or top to hug the status bar. Adjust only if the default placement looks off for your header height.

subarticles.title: Skip Button Label
subarticles.summary: Sets the text and styling of the Skip control that lets visitors bypass this step. Defaults to 'SKIP' and supports other languages. Use it only where skipping is fine, and clear it to hide it on your paywall and key question screens, where an easy out lowers both sales and the answers you collect.

subarticles.title: Skip button text style
subarticles.summary: Overrides how the Skip control's label looks — font, size, weight, color, alignment, line height, an optional highlight, and a strikethrough color. By default it inherits your theme. Keep Skip visually quiet (smaller, lower-contrast) so it doesn't pull attention away from continuing; restyle it only to fit a specific header look.

subarticles.title: Media — every setting
subarticles.summary: The screen's image or video block — its source, size, placement, rounding, and an optional fade overlay. This guide documents every setting of the Media block, grouped by area. Each setting matches a real control in the screen editor.

subarticles.title: Media section
subarticles.summary: The Media section adds an image or video that supports the screen's message: a product shot, a before/after, or a short explainer clip. On a paid landing page strong visuals build trust and lift conversion, but keep them relevant so they reinforce the headline instead of distracting from the choice or button the visitor needs to act on. It shows on choice screens and the wheel picker; headline screens set their image inside the Content section instead.

subarticles.title: Where it appears
subarticles.summary: Covered screen types: ListMultiPick, ListSinglePick, GridMultiPick, GridSinglePick, WheelPicker.

subarticles.title: How rounded the media is
subarticles.summary: Rounds the corners of the media block; 0 is sharp and higher values (up to 50) make them softer. A small radius around 8 to 16 gives a modern, polished look; match it to the rounding on your buttons and cards so the whole screen feels consistent. Leave it at 0 for full-bleed media that touches the screen edges.

subarticles.title: Show an image or video
subarticles.summary: Turns the image or video block on or off for this screen; off means no visual is shown. Turn it on to add a supporting visual, since on a paid landing page a relevant image or video builds trust and lifts conversion. When enabled, it starts with sensible styling from your design theme that you can fine-tune in the fields below.

subarticles.title: Color of the fade
subarticles.summary: Picks the color of the fade over the media. Use a dark color (usually black) behind light or white text, or a light color behind dark text; the fade goes from this color to fully transparent so the image still shows through. Match it to your background or brand color for a seamless look, and choose whichever direction gives your copy the strongest contrast.

subarticles.title: Fade over the media
subarticles.summary: Lays a soft, see-through fade (usually dark) over the media so any text or button on top stays readable against a busy image. Turn it on whenever you place a title, subtitle, or button over the media; without it, light areas of the image can wash out your copy. When enabled, you get controls below to set the fade's height and color.

subarticles.title: How far the fade extends
subarticles.summary: Controls how far the fade reaches across the media (0 to 100%). Match it to where your text or button sits: if the copy is near the bottom, a 30 to 50% fade from that edge usually gives enough contrast without darkening the whole image. Increase it if text is still hard to read, decrease it to show more of the image clearly.

subarticles.title: How tall the media is
subarticles.summary: Sets the media height as a share of the screen (0 to 100%), so it scales on every device; the default is 50%. Use a larger percentage for an immersive, image-led screen and a smaller one when you need room for the title, text, or button below; on a choice screen, keep it modest so the options stay visible without scrolling. Setting a value pins the media just below the header for a consistent layout.

subarticles.title: The image for this screen
subarticles.summary: Add this screen's image by uploading a file from your computer or pasting a direct image URL, then confirm it in the preview. Use a high-quality JPG or PNG that's on-message for the screen — uploads are optimized automatically for fast loading on every device. To replace it later, upload or paste a new source here.

subarticles.title: Image or video
subarticles.summary: Pick whether this screen shows an image or a video. Use an image for a fast, lightweight visual that loads instantly; use a video for short product demos or motion that holds attention (it can loop). Switching type clears the current media, so choose before you upload. Keep videos short and light so the page stays fast, since slow loads cost conversions on paid traffic.

subarticles.title: Space around the media
subarticles.summary: Adds empty space on the four sides of the media (top, right, bottom, left) so it isn't flush against the screen edges or neighboring content. Leave it at the default for a full-width visual. Increase a side to inset the media and give it a framed look with breathing room, rather than edge-to-edge.

subarticles.title: How media fills its box
subarticles.summary: Controls how the media fills its box. Aspect Fit shows the whole thing without cropping (you may see empty bars), Aspect Fill covers the box completely but may crop edges, and Scale to Fill stretches it, which distorts photos, so avoid that. The positional options (Top, Bottom, Center, and so on) crop to fill while keeping that part in view. Aspect Fill is the usual pick for an edge-to-edge banner; use Aspect Fit when nothing should be cropped.

subarticles.title: Where the media starts on top
subarticles.summary: Sets where the media begins from the top of the screen. Screen Top runs it edge-to-edge to the very top (great for a full-bleed hero), Navigation Bar starts it just below the header, and Safe Area keeps it clear of phone notches and rounded corners. Pick Screen Top for an immersive banner, Safe Area when nothing should ever be clipped. This is locked if you set a media height percentage below, which positions it for you.

subarticles.title: Replay the video on a loop
subarticles.summary: When on, the video replays continuously; when off, it plays once and stops on the last frame. Only applies to video media. Turn looping on for short ambient background clips that hold attention; turn it off for a demo or explainer you want watched once, so it doesn't loop distractingly while the visitor reads.

subarticles.title: The video for this screen
subarticles.summary: Add a video by uploading a file or pasting a direct video URL. Keep it short (a few seconds, ideally under ~30s) and lightweight so the page loads fast — long or heavy videos hurt conversion on paid traffic. Uploads are converted automatically to play reliably across devices, and you can pair this with the loop option below to replay it continuously.

subarticles.summary: The answer choices visitors pick from — selection mode, list-or-grid layout, item states, spacing, and styling. This guide documents every setting of the Options block, grouped by area. Each setting matches a real control in the screen editor.

subarticles.title: Options section
subarticles.summary: The Options section defines the answer choices, product cards, or tappable rows a visitor picks from on a selection screen. This is the core interaction that captures what the visitor wants, so pair it with Variable Binding to save each choice and use it to personalize copy and send the visitor toward the right paywall. If a screen has no Options section, it isn't a selection screen; add a list or grid screen from the canvas.

subarticles.title: Where it appears
subarticles.summary: Covered screen types: ListMultiPick, ListSinglePick, GridMultiPick, GridSinglePick, HeroList.

subarticles.title: Grid cell proportions
subarticles.summary: Sets each grid cell's height as a percentage of its width: 100 is square, above 100 makes taller cells, below 100 makes wider, shorter cells. Pick taller cells for image-led options and square for balanced icon-and-text choices. Only appears on two-column grids — try 100 first, then adjust to fit your content.

subarticles.title: Checkbox placement in grid cells
subarticles.summary: On grid cells, show or hide the selection checkbox and place it in a corner (top-left, top-right, bottom-left, or bottom-right) with an optional offset. Keep it visible on multi-select grids so visitors can see what they've picked; top-right is a common, unobtrusive spot. Only appears on grid layouts.

subarticles.title: Checkbox look
subarticles.summary: Appearance of the selection checkbox — shape (square or circle), checked color, unchecked color, and padding. Use your theme's accent for the checked color so a tap reads clearly as selected, matching the selected-item look. Circle suits pick-one (radio style), square suits multi-select. Only appears when the layout includes a checkbox or on grids.

subarticles.title: List or grid layout
subarticles.summary: Choose whether choices stack in a single-column list or sit in a two-column grid. Use a list for text-heavy answers that need a full line each; use a grid when items have images or icons and you want a compact, visual picker. Switching to a grid unlocks the image, text, and checkbox layout controls. Default to a single-column list for plain answer choices.

subarticles.title: Image area in each card
subarticles.summary: On grid cards that show an image, this sets the image region as a whole: where it sits in the card, how tall it is (a fixed height or sized to fit its content), and the spacing around it. By default it fits the content, but setting one fixed height keeps every card's image lined up at the same level, which looks more polished and trustworthy on an ad landing page. This shapes the image's container only; the image's own size and corners are set separately in the item image styles.

subarticles.title: Item image look
subarticles.summary: Size and look of each item's image — width, height, corner radius, padding, and how it fits its box (fit shows the whole image with possible empty space; fill crops to cover the box). Keep a consistent size and small radius so cards look uniform; choose fill for photos and fit for logos or icons you don't want cropped. Only appears when the layout includes an image.

subarticles.title: What each choice shows
subarticles.summary: Pick which parts each choice displays — title only, image plus title, checkbox with title and subtitle, and so on; available combos depend on your selection mode and layout. Adding an element reveals its style controls and means you must supply that content (image or subtitle) on every item. Default to title (plus a checkbox for multi-select) and add an image only when it aids the choice.

subarticles.title: Padding inside each item
subarticles.summary: The space between each item's edge and its content (title, image, checkbox), set per side — top, end, bottom, start. More padding makes items feel roomy and easier to tap; too little looks cramped. Around 12–16px on all sides reads well on mobile, and the setting applies to every item.

subarticles.title: Gap between choices
subarticles.summary: The spacing between adjacent choices — a vertical gap in lists, the gap between cells in grids. Around 8–12px keeps items clearly separate and easy to tap without wasting space. Increase it for a more airy feel, or decrease it to fit more options above the fold.

subarticles.title: Margin around the whole list
subarticles.summary: The outer space between the screen edges and the first and last items, set per side (top, end, bottom, start). Use it to keep the list off the screen edges and aligned with your other sections. This is the outside spacing — for the gap inside each item use Padding inside each item instead.

subarticles.title: Even grid cell heights
subarticles.summary: On a grid, choose whether all cells stretch to the same maximum height for tidy, even rows, or each cell sizes to its own content (giving rows of varying height). Turn it on for a clean, consistent grid; turn it off when items have very different content lengths. Only applies to grid layouts.

subarticles.title: Cap on multi-select picks
subarticles.summary: Limits how many items a visitor can choose on a multi-select screen. Set a small cap (e.g. 3) to keep answers focused and the next step manageable; leave it unlimited to let them pick freely. This control only appears on multi-select screens and is ignored everywhere else.

subarticles.title: Shuffle item order
subarticles.summary: When enabled, randomizes the order items appear to users on each view. Useful for A/B testing, survey randomization, and reducing position bias in multi-select scenarios.

subarticles.title: Selected item look
subarticles.summary: How a choice looks once tapped — background, border, corner radius, and optional gradient. Make it clearly distinct from the unselected look (an accent border or filled background) so visitors get instant confirmation; weak feedback here causes hesitation and drop-off. Your theme's accent color is a reliable choice.

subarticles.title: How visitors choose
subarticles.summary: Sets how people interact: browse only (no selection, like an intro list), pick one, or pick several. This also decides what's saved to the bound variable — pick-one stores a single value you can branch on, pick-several stores a set. Default to pick-one for most onboarding questions.

subarticles.title: Item subtitle text style
subarticles.summary: Typography for the item subtitle — size, weight, color, alignment, line height, optional background, and padding, applied to all items as a shared template. Keep the subtitle visually quieter than the title (smaller, muted color) so it reads as supporting text. Only appears when your item layout includes a subtitle.

subarticles.title: Text area in each card
subarticles.summary: On grid cards with an image, this sets the title-and-subtitle region as a block: where it sits in the card, how tall it is (a fixed height or sized to fit its content), and the spacing around it. It fits the content by default, but choosing one fixed height keeps the text blocks aligned across every card so the row reads as a clean, scannable set. This controls the text region's position only; the actual fonts and colors of the title and subtitle are set in their own style sections.

subarticles.title: Item title text style
subarticles.summary: Typography for every item's title — size, weight, color, alignment, line height, plus an optional background chip (color, opacity, radius) and padding. It's a shared template, so an edit restyles all items at once. Leave it on theme defaults for consistency, adjusting size or color only to improve readability against the item background.

subarticles.title: Unselected item look
subarticles.summary: The default look of each choice before it's tapped — background, border, corner radius, and an optional gradient. Keep it neutral and calm so the selected state can stand out; the contrast between this and the selected look is what tells visitors their tap registered. Pair it with the Selected item look.

subarticles.title: Vertical alignment of items
subarticles.summary: Aligns each choice's content to the top, center, or bottom of its cell. It's most noticeable in grid layouts where cells are taller than their content; center usually looks balanced. In simple lists it has little visible effect, so center is a safe default.

subarticles.title: Paywall Body — every setting
subarticles.summary: The paywall's words — the headline and subtitle (with full typography) and the feature-benefit bullet list, including each bullet's box style, padding, and per-bullet title / subtitle / icon styling. This guide documents every setting of the Paywall Body block, grouped by area. Each setting matches a real control in the screen editor.

subarticles.title: Paywall Body section
subarticles.summary: The Paywall Body is the persuasion area above the plan cards, where you write the title, subtitle, and feature bullets that explain why the offer is worth paying for. Keep the title to one clear benefit and use the bullets for proof like guarantees and what's included, since this copy is what lifts conversion before the visitor ever looks at the price. Edit it on any paywall screen, ideally after connecting Stripe so the benefits you promise match the plans on sale.

subarticles.title: Where it appears
subarticles.summary: Covered screen types: Paywall.

subarticles.title: Style the bullet icons
subarticles.summary: Styles the small icon or image on each bullet: how it sits in its box (fit shows the whole image, fill crops it to cover), how rounded the corners are, and the spacing around it, applied to all bullets at once. Keep icon size and shape consistent so the checklist looks tidy. The theme defaults are a safe start.

subarticles.title: Style the bullet subtitles
subarticles.summary: Styles the secondary line under each bullet title: font, size, weight, color, alignment, and spacing, applied to all bullets at once. Keep it smaller and lighter than the bullet title so the benefit itself stays the focus. Leave the theme defaults unless the text is hard to read.

subarticles.title: Style the bullet titles
subarticles.summary: Styles the main line of every feature bullet: font, size, weight, color, alignment, and spacing, applied to all bullets at once. Keep bullet titles bold and easy to read so each benefit lands at a glance. The theme defaults usually work, so change them only if a benefit is hard to read.

subarticles.title: Benefit checklist
subarticles.summary: The list of benefits below the subtitle, your main proof the offer is worth paying for. Add one bullet per concrete benefit (what's included, guarantees, results), each with a title, optional subtitle, and icon, and drag to reorder. Aim for 3 to 5 punchy bullets, since too many dilute the message. Use 'Add Bullet' to create one, or clone an existing bullet to keep the styling consistent.

subarticles.title: Space inside each bullet
subarticles.summary: Sets the breathing room inside each bullet, between its text or icon and the bullet's edge, adjustable on the top, bottom, left, and right. Increase it if bullets feel cramped, decrease it to fit more on screen. The theme default is usually fine, so tweak only if the spacing looks off in preview.

subarticles.title: Style the feature bullets
subarticles.summary: Sets the background color, border, and corner rounding applied to every bullet in the list at once. Use a subtle card background or border only if you want the bullets to read as a grouped card; otherwise the theme defaults look cleanest. Styling once keeps all bullets consistent.

subarticles.title: Space around the bullet list
subarticles.summary: Sets the space around the whole list of bullets, separating it from the subtitle above and the plans below. (Bullet padding spaces the inside of one bullet; this spaces the entire group.) Add space if the list feels jammed against the title or the plan cards; the theme default is a safe start.

subarticles.title: Style the paywall subtitle
subarticles.summary: Styles the subtitle line: font, size, weight, color, alignment, and the spacing around it. Keep it smaller and lighter than the headline so the main benefit stays dominant. Leave the theme defaults unless the subtitle is hard to read against your background.

subarticles.title: Supporting subtitle
subarticles.summary: The supporting line just under the headline. Use it to back up the promise with a reason to believe or a specific outcome (e.g. 'Cancel anytime, no questions asked'). You can drop in @variables to reference the user's earlier answers for a personal touch. Turn it off to hide the subtitle.

subarticles.title: Style the paywall headline
subarticles.summary: Styles the headline: font, size, weight, color, alignment, and the spacing around it. Keep it large and high-contrast so the main benefit is the first thing the eye lands on. Most users can leave the theme defaults; change them only if the title is hard to read against your background.

subarticles.title: Paywall headline
subarticles.summary: The big headline at the top of the paywall, your one shot to state your strongest benefit in a few words (e.g. 'Reach your goal in 4 weeks'). You can insert @variables like @{user.name} to echo answers the user gave earlier, which makes the offer feel personal and lifts conversion. Turn it off to hide the headline entirely.

subarticles.title: Paywall Footer — every setting
subarticles.summary: The bottom of the paywall — the purchase (subscribe) button and its label and box styling, the auto-renew disclosure note, the footer background and element order, and the restore / terms-of-use / privacy-policy legal links with their URLs and styling. This guide documents every setting of the Paywall Footer block, grouped by area. Each setting matches a real control in the screen editor.

subarticles.title: Paywall Footer section
subarticles.summary: The Paywall Footer is the bottom action zone of a paywall and holds your single most important conversion control: the purchase/subscribe button, plus the auto-renew disclosure and legal links (Restore, Terms of Use, Privacy Policy). For an ad-ready paywall you must have a working purchase button and filled-in Terms and Privacy links, because ad networks and app stores reject paywalls without them. It only appears on paywall screens.

subarticles.title: Where it appears
subarticles.summary: Covered screen types: Paywall.

subarticles.title: Auto-renew text spacing
subarticles.summary: Adds padding around the auto-renew disclosure text on each side — top, bottom, left, and right (left/right flip for right-to-left languages). The defaults are fine for most paywalls; this is optional fine-tuning. Add a little top spacing if you want to separate the disclosure from the button above it.

subarticles.title: Auto-renew disclosure styling
subarticles.summary: Sets the font, size, weight, color, and alignment of the auto-renew disclosure text. Keep it small and quiet relative to your main button — but it must stay clearly readable. App Store and ad-network rules require the renewal terms be legible, so avoid tiny sizes or low-contrast colors that effectively hide the disclosure.

subarticles.title: Configure auto-renew disclosure text
subarticles.summary: Sets the text displayed below the purchase button to explain subscription renewal terms (default: Auto-renews monthly. Cancel anytime.). Supports template variables like duration, price, and custom links.

subarticles.title: Color the footer background
subarticles.summary: Sets the fill color of the whole footer block, which holds the purchase button, the auto-renew note, and the legal links (default a dark tone). Pick a color that makes your button pop and keeps the renewal note and legal links readable. If you switch to a light footer, darken those text colors so everything stays legible.

subarticles.title: Order the button and renewal note
subarticles.summary: Sets whether the purchase button sits above the auto-renew disclosure or below it. Button-first is the common, conversion-friendly default. Put the disclosure first when you want the renewal terms visible right above the button so users read them before tapping — often the safer choice for compliance.

subarticles.title: Legal links row spacing
subarticles.summary: Adds padding around the whole row of legal links — Restore, Terms, and Privacy together — on each side: top, bottom, left, and right (left/right flip for right-to-left languages). The defaults are fine; this is optional fine-tuning. Add a little top and bottom spacing so the links sit clearly below the disclosure without crowding.

subarticles.title: Privacy link styling
subarticles.summary: Sets the font, size, weight, color, and alignment of the Privacy Policy link. Match it to the Restore and Terms links so the legal row looks unified. Small and muted is fine, but it must stay readable — required legal links hidden in unreadable text can get your paywall rejected.

subarticles.title: Configure privacy policy link
subarticles.summary: Sets the text for the privacy policy link (default: Privacy Policy). This link appears in the legal links section and navigates to your privacy document when tapped.

subarticles.title: Link your Privacy Policy page
subarticles.summary: The full https:// web address your Privacy Policy link opens when tapped. Fill this in for any paid funnel — a live Privacy Policy is required by app stores and ad platforms once you collect payment or data. Leaving it empty disables the link and leaves the paywall non-compliant, so don't publish an ad-ready paywall with this blank.

subarticles.title: Style the purchase button box
subarticles.summary: Controls the look of the purchase button itself — fill color, border, corner radius, size, full-width toggle, padding, gradient, shadow, animation, and icon (the label text is styled separately). For ad funnels, a full-width button with a high-contrast accent fill and rounded corners is the proven setup. Make this the boldest element on the screen so the path to purchase is unmistakable.

subarticles.title: Recover users who cancel checkout
subarticles.summary: Lets you send people who start checkout but back out to a cheaper plan or discount offer instead of just closing the dialog. Catching abandoners this way can recover lost revenue, but you must build that follow-up screen first and connect it here. Leave it empty until you have one — then the dialog simply closes and the user stays on the paywall.

subarticles.title: Set space inside the button
subarticles.summary: Sets the padding between the button's label and its edges — top, bottom, left, and right (left/right swap automatically for right-to-left languages). Use generous top and bottom padding so the button feels large and tappable. A cramped call-to-action looks less clickable and lowers taps on mobile.

subarticles.title: Style the purchase button label
subarticles.summary: Controls the look of the text inside the purchase button — font, size, weight, color, alignment, and spacing — not the button box itself, which you style under 'Style purchase button box and appearance'. This is your main call-to-action, so make the label large, bold, and high-contrast against the button fill. Weak or hard-to-read button text directly costs you taps and sales.

subarticles.title: Configure purchase button text
subarticles.summary: Sets the visible label on the purchase subscribe button (default: Subscribe Now). The text supports template variables like pricing, duration, and custom countdown labels for dynamic personalization.

subarticles.title: Restore link styling
subarticles.summary: Sets the font, size, weight, color, and alignment of the footer 'Restore Purchases' link. Style it to match the Terms and Privacy links beside it so the legal row reads as one consistent group — small and muted, but still legible. Don't make it look like your main button.

subarticles.title: Configure restore purchases link
subarticles.summary: Sets the text for the restore purchases link (default: Restore Purchases). This link appears in the legal links section below the auto-renew label and allows users to restore prior subscriptions on iOS.

subarticles.title: Terms link styling
subarticles.summary: Sets the font, size, weight, color, and alignment of the Terms of Use link. Keep it consistent with the Restore and Privacy links beside it — small and muted is fine, but it must stay readable. Burying required legal links in unreadable micro-text invites store rejection and ad-network flags.

subarticles.title: Configure terms of use link
subarticles.summary: Sets the text for the terms of use link (default: Terms of Use). This link appears in the legal links section and navigates to your terms document when tapped.

subarticles.title: Link your Terms of Use page
subarticles.summary: The full https:// web address your Terms of Use link opens when tapped. Fill this in for any paid funnel — a live Terms link is effectively required by app stores and ad networks. Leaving it empty disables the link and leaves your paywall non-compliant, so never ship an ad-ready paywall with this blank.

subarticles.title: Paywall Header — every setting
subarticles.summary: The paywall's top bar — an optional close (X) button (its icon color, which side it sits on, and whether it appears at once or after a short delay) and an optional restore-purchases link with its own wording and typography. This guide documents every setting of the Paywall Header block, grouped by area. Each setting matches a real control in the screen editor.

subarticles.title: Paywall Header section
subarticles.summary: The Paywall Header is the top strip of a paywall screen. Use it for the close (X) button and an optional 'Restore Purchases' label, and to style their color, position, and timing. Keep it minimal — a clear way to close plus restore is enough for an ad-ready paywall, since anything extra up here pulls attention away from the offer below. It only appears on paywall screens.

subarticles.title: Where it appears
subarticles.summary: Covered screen types: Paywall.

subarticles.title: Place the close button left or right
subarticles.summary: Puts the X on the start side (left in most languages, right in right-to-left ones) or the end side of the header; the sides flip automatically by language. Default to the start/top-left to match common mobile paywall convention. Move it to the end only when your hero layout needs that corner kept clear.

subarticles.title: Show a close (X) button
subarticles.summary: Adds the X in the header that lets people dismiss the paywall and keep browsing. For paid-ad traffic keep it on (optionally with a short reveal delay) — an inescapable paywall hurts trust and can break app-store and ad-network rules. Turn it off only when you deliberately want a hard gate users can't skip.

subarticles.title: How long to delay the X
subarticles.summary: How long the close button stays hidden (1-30 seconds) when you've set it to appear after a timer; it has no effect otherwise. A short 2-3 seconds nudges users to read the offer first without feeling trapped. Longer delays raise frustration and drop-off, so reserve 10s or more only for a deliberate hard gate.

subarticles.title: Color the close (X) icon
subarticles.summary: Sets the color of the X dismiss icon (default white; applies only when the close button is shown). Choose a color that contrasts with whatever sits behind the header — dark over a light hero image, white over a dark one — so users can always find and tap it. Low contrast here can leave people feeling trapped on the paywall.

subarticles.title: When the close button appears
subarticles.summary: Controls when the X becomes tappable: right away, or after a short timer that lets users take in the offer first (set the length in the delay field below). For ad traffic, showing it immediately or after a 2-3 second delay converts well without feeling like a trap. Avoid long delays that frustrate users or break ad-network rules.

subarticles.title: Restore link background fill
subarticles.summary: Adds a colored background block behind the restore link text. Most restore links sit on the plain header with no fill, so the default is none — leave it unset for the usual text-only look. Set a color only if you want a chip or pill behind the link, then shape it with the opacity and corner-radius fields below.

subarticles.title: Restore background transparency
subarticles.summary: Controls how see-through the restore link's background fill is, from 0 (invisible) to 1 (solid). It only has an effect once you've set a background color above. Use a partial value for a faint chip behind the text so it stays readable over a busy hero image; otherwise leave it alone.

subarticles.title: Restore background rounding
subarticles.summary: Rounds the corners of the restore link's background block, from 0 (sharp rectangle) up to 50 (full pill). It only shows once you've given the link a background color and opacity. Use a higher value for a pill-shaped chip; the default of 0 is fine, and you can ignore it entirely if there's no background fill.

subarticles.title: Show a restore-purchases link
subarticles.summary: Adds a small 'Restore Purchases' control in the header so returning buyers can recover an existing subscription instead of paying twice. Keep it on: a working restore option is effectively required on app-store paywalls and it reassures buyers, which protects conversions. There's also a Restore link available in the footer legal links, so use whichever placement fits your layout.

subarticles.title: Pick the restore link typeface
subarticles.summary: Chooses the font for the restore link (SF Pro, SF Pro Rounded, SF Mono, or New York; default SF Pro). Match it to the font used elsewhere on the paywall so the screen looks consistent and trustworthy. There's rarely a reason to give the restore link its own typeface, so SF Pro is a safe choice.

subarticles.title: Size the restore link text
subarticles.summary: Sets how large the restore link reads, in points (0-50). Keep it small and secondary — around 12-14pt — so it stays legible but doesn't compete with your headline or purchase button. Restore is a recovery option, not a primary action, so resist sizing it up.

subarticles.title: Set the restore link boldness
subarticles.summary: Controls how heavy the restore link text looks (for example Normal or Semibold). Use a normal weight so restore stays a quiet secondary link and doesn't pull attention from your purchase button. Bump it to semibold only if it's genuinely hard to read against the background.

subarticles.title: Restore link line spacing
subarticles.summary: Sets the vertical space between lines of the restore text. The link is almost always one short line, so this usually has no visible effect — leave it at the default. Only raise it slightly if your custom restore text wraps to multiple lines and the lines look crowded.

subarticles.title: Restore link strikethrough color
subarticles.summary: Colors a line struck through the restore text, but only if you have deliberately added a crossed-out segment to that text. A standard 'Restore Purchases' link has no strikethrough, so leave this alone — it does nothing unless your custom text actually contains a struck-through part.

subarticles.title: Align the restore link text
subarticles.summary: Sets where the restore link sits in its row — start (left in most languages), center, or end (right) — flipping automatically for right-to-left languages. Usually align it to the side opposite the close button, or center it, so the header reads cleanly. The default works for most layouts.

subarticles.title: Color the restore link text
subarticles.summary: Sets the restore link's text color (default a muted gray). Check it against your header background first — that gray default disappears on a dark hero, so use a lighter tint there. Keep it readable but understated so restore reads as a secondary link, with enough contrast to stay accessible.

subarticles.title: Edit the restore link wording
subarticles.summary: The text shown on the header restore link, editable for each language you support (default 'Restore Purchases'). Keep it close to the standard 'Restore Purchases' wording so returning buyers instantly recognize it. Add other-language versions only if your funnel actually ships in multiple languages.

subarticles.title: Show a close (X) button

For paid-ad traffic keep it on (optionally with a short reveal delay) — an inescapable paywall hurts trust and can break app-store and ad-network rules. Turn it off only when you deliberately want a hard gate users can't skip.

subarticles.title: Color the close (X) icon
subarticles.summary: Sets the color of the X dismiss icon (default white; applies only when the close button is shown). Choose a color that contrasts with whatever sits behind the header — dark over a light hero image, white over a dark one — so users can always find and tap it. Low contrast here can leave people feeling trapped on the paywall.

subarticles.title: Paywall Media — every setting
subarticles.summary: The paywall's featured image or video — its source, how it fills its area, height, corner rounding, spacing, where it sits relative to the header and body, and an optional dark fade overlay for text readability. This guide documents every setting of the Paywall Media block, grouped by area. Each setting matches a real control in the screen editor.

subarticles.title: Paywall Media section
subarticles.summary: The Paywall Media section is the featured image or video at the top of the paywall that visually sells the offer — a product shot, before/after, or short demo. Choose Image or Video and upload your asset, then check the preview so it reinforces the promise without pushing the plan cards and purchase button out of view on a phone. A relevant, high-quality visual builds trust, while an irrelevant one just wastes screen space.

subarticles.title: Where it appears
subarticles.summary: Covered screen types: Paywall.

subarticles.title: How media meets the text
subarticles.summary: Sets how the media and the paywall text relate vertically. 'Above Content' keeps the media as a banner with the title, subtitle, and plans stacked below it (safest, always readable); 'Behind Intro Content' layers the title over the media for a magazine-style hero. Start with Above Content; if you choose the overlaid look, turn on the gradient overlay so the text stays legible.

subarticles.title: Round the media corners
subarticles.summary: Sets how rounded the corners of the image or video are. Zero gives sharp edges, which often look best for a full-width hero, while higher values give a soft, card-like look that matches rounded buttons and plan cards. Match it to the rest of your theme's rounding; the default is usually fine.

subarticles.title: Show featured media
subarticles.summary: Turn this on to show a featured image or video at the top of the paywall, or off to hide media and give the plan cards more room. After enabling, choose the media type and upload your asset, otherwise nothing appears. Use media when a visual strengthens the offer; skip it for a tighter, text-only paywall.

subarticles.title: Gradient overlay color
subarticles.summary: Sets the color of the dark fade laid over your media (default black). Black works best behind white text; choose a dark brand color if you want the fade to feel on-theme. The overlay always fades to clear at the top, so only this base color matters. It appears only when the gradient overlay is turned on.

subarticles.title: Gradient coverage
subarticles.summary: How far up the media the dark fade reaches, as a percentage. A low value shades only the bottom edge (enough for text sitting near the bottom); a high value darkens most of the image. Set it just high enough to cover where your overlaid text sits, leaving the rest of the image visible. This only appears when the gradient overlay is turned on.

subarticles.title: Dark fade over media
subarticles.summary: Lays a dark fade over the image or video so any text and buttons placed on top stay readable. Turn it on whenever you layer the headline or content over the media, or when a busy or light image makes text hard to read; leave it off for a clean image with nothing on top. Once on, you can fine-tune its height and color below.

subarticles.title: Media height on screen
subarticles.summary: How much of the screen the featured image or video takes up, as a share of screen height. Keep it moderate (around 30 to 45%) so the plan cards and purchase button stay visible without scrolling; too tall pushes your offer below the fold and costs you sales. Always check the result on a phone-sized preview.

subarticles.title: Upload the featured image
subarticles.summary: Upload (or clear) the hero image shown at the top of the paywall. Use a high-resolution image with its subject centered, since the edges may be cropped depending on your fit setting. If your funnel runs in multiple languages you can upload a different image per language; it appears only when media type is Image, and nothing shows until you upload one.

subarticles.title: Image or video
subarticles.summary: Picks whether the featured media is an image or a video. Image is simplest and loads fastest; video can show your product in motion but should be short and auto-playing. Note that switching type clears any asset you already uploaded, so choose first, then upload; picking Video also unlocks the loop option.

subarticles.title: Space around the media
subarticles.summary: Sets the space between the media and its surroundings on each side: top, right, bottom, and left. Add padding to inset the image or video from the screen edges for a framed look, or set it to zero for a full-bleed, edge-to-edge hero. The theme default is a safe start; adjust only if the media looks too tight or too floaty in preview.

subarticles.title: Loop the video
subarticles.summary: When on, the featured video repeats continuously; when off, it plays once and stops on the last frame. Loop short, ambient clips (a few seconds) so the paywall stays lively and eye-catching; turn it off for a video with a clear ending you don't want replayed. This only appears when the media type is Video.

subarticles.title: How the media fills its area
subarticles.summary: Decides how your image or video sits in its space. 'Fit' shows the whole asset but may leave blank bars around it; 'Fill' crops the edges so the area is covered with no gaps. Fill usually looks best for a clean edge-to-edge hero, just keep anything important away from the edges; choose Fit only when the entire image must stay visible.

subarticles.title: Where media starts vertically
subarticles.summary: Sets where the image or video begins at the top of the screen relative to the header (back button and progress bar). 'Screen Top' starts media at the very top behind the header for a full-bleed hero look; 'Header Bottom' starts it just under the header so the controls stay clear of the image. Use Header Bottom if the header overlaps your media awkwardly, otherwise Screen Top is the most immersive.

subarticles.title: Upload the featured video
subarticles.summary: Upload (or clear) the hero video shown at the top of the paywall. Keep it short and lightweight (a few seconds, compressed) so it loads fast on mobile data, and remember it auto-plays muted, so the visual must work without sound. If your funnel runs in multiple languages you can upload a different video per language; it appears only when media type is Video, and nothing shows until you upload one.

It covers linked Stripe products, product catalog items, selection state, item labels, pricing text, subscription options, layout, styling, and ordinary paywall purchase behavior.

subarticles.title: Plan card appearance & spacing
subarticles.summary: Plan card appearance & spacing

subarticles.title: Plans & arrangement
subarticles.summary: Plans & arrangement

subarticles.title: Per-plan labels, badge & checkbox
subarticles.summary: Per-plan labels, badge & checkbox

subarticles.title: Paywall Subscriptions — every setting
subarticles.summary: The plan picker — how the subscription cards are arranged, where the selection checkbox sits, the plans themselves, the selected/unselected card styling and spacing, and each plan's name / price / note / billing-period labels, badge, and checkbox styling. This guide documents every setting of the Paywall Subscriptions block, grouped by area. Each setting matches a real control in the screen editor.

subarticles.title: Paywall Subscriptions section
subarticles.summary: The Paywall Subscriptions section is where you list the plans a visitor can buy. Each plan row is tied to a real product in your connected Stripe account, so the price and billing period shown here must match an actual Stripe product or checkout will fail. Add one row per plan, pre-select the option you most want sold (usually the annual or best-value plan) to boost conversion, and set this up after connecting Stripe and creating your products.

subarticles.title: Where it appears
subarticles.summary: Covered screen types: Paywall.

subarticles.title: Plan badge
subarticles.summary: An optional ribbon on a plan card, like 'Most Popular' or 'Best Value', used to steer attention to the plan you most want sold. The styling (color, border, position, spacing) is shared across all plans, but the badge text is set per plan, so add text only to the one plan you're promoting. A single well-placed badge lifts conversion; badging every plan cancels the effect.

subarticles.title: Style the billing period (bottom-right)
subarticles.summary: Styles the bottom-right label on every plan card, usually the billing period like 'per month': font, size, weight, color, alignment, and spacing, applied to all plans at once. The text follows the linked product; this only sets the look. Keep it small and quiet under the price; theme defaults are a safe start.

subarticles.title: Style the plan note (bottom-left)
subarticles.summary: Styles the bottom-left label on every plan card, usually the short plan description or trial note: font, size, weight, color, alignment, and spacing, applied to all plans at once. This sets only the look; you write the actual text per plan in the plan list. Keep it smaller and lighter than the plan name; theme defaults are a safe start.

subarticles.title: Style the plan checkbox
subarticles.summary: Sets the colors of the per-plan checkbox: its unselected (empty) color and its selected (checked) color. It only appears when checkbox placement is set to Left or Right, and is hidden when placement is 'No checkbox'. Use a clear, on-brand selected color so the chosen plan is unmistakable; it defaults to your theme accent.

subarticles.title: Plan name vs. price width
subarticles.summary: Sets how much of each plan card's width goes to the left labels (plan name and description), leaving the rest for the right labels (price and billing period). Around 60-70% usually gives names enough room while keeping prices aligned on the right. Lower it if prices look cramped, raise it if plan names wrap awkwardly.

subarticles.title: Space inside each plan card
subarticles.summary: Sets the padding inside each plan card, between its labels and the card edge, on the top, bottom, left, and right. Increase it to make cards feel roomier and easier to tap, decrease it to fit more plans on screen. The theme default is usually fine; adjust only if cards look cramped in preview.

subarticles.title: Subscription plans
subarticles.summary: The list of plans the user can buy. Each plan must be linked to a real product in your connected Stripe account, or checkout will fail when you publish. Per plan you set its four corner labels (top-left = plan name, bottom-left = description, top-right = price, bottom-right = billing period) and an optional badge. Mark your best-value plan as selected by default, since the pre-selected plan converts most often. Use 'Add Plan' to add rows.

subarticles.title: Space around the plan list
subarticles.summary: Sets the space around the whole block of plans, between the list and the screen edges and the content above and below it. (Card padding spaces the inside of one plan; this spaces the entire group.) Add space if the plans feel jammed against the body copy or the purchase button; the theme default is a safe start.

subarticles.title: Checkbox placement on plans
subarticles.summary: Choose where the selection checkbox sits on each plan card: left, right, or hidden. Left or right makes selecting a plan obvious; Hidden removes the checkbox and lets the highlighted card itself signal the choice for a cleaner look, but only if your selected style is clearly distinct. Left is a safe default. This also works together with the checkbox styling field below.

subarticles.title: Selected plan style
subarticles.summary: How a plan card looks once it's the chosen one: background color, border, and spacing. Make it clearly stand out from the unselected cards, for example a brand-colored border or filled background, so the user is never unsure which plan they're about to buy. Crisp selected styling removes hesitation right before checkout.

subarticles.title: Style the price (top-right)
subarticles.summary: Styles the top-right label on every plan card, usually the price: font, size, weight, color, alignment, and spacing, applied to all plans at once. The price value itself comes from the linked Stripe product, not here. Make the price bold and prominent so it's easy to compare across plans; theme defaults usually work.

subarticles.title: Style the plan name (top-left)
subarticles.summary: Styles the top-left label on every plan card, which usually holds the plan name like 'Annual': font, size, weight, color, alignment, and spacing, applied to all plans at once. This only controls how it looks; you edit each plan's actual name in the plan list. Make plan names bold and legible so they're easy to compare; theme defaults usually work.

subarticles.title: Unselected plan style
subarticles.summary: How a plan card looks before the user taps it: background color, border, and spacing. Keep this neutral and understated so the chosen plan can clearly stand out against it. The contrast between this and the Selected style is what tells users which plan they've picked, so never make the two look the same.

subarticles.title: Plan card arrangement
subarticles.summary: Choose how the plan cards are laid out. Vertical stacks them one under another, which reads best on mobile and works well for 2 to 4 plans; Horizontal lines them up side by side as compact cards, good for 2 short price options you want compared at a glance. subarticles.title: Roller — every setting
subarticles.summary: A spinning wheel picker — the data type, the wheels and their values (text lists or number ranges), the selected-value label styling, and the picker container’s background, borders, corner radius and padding. This guide documents every setting of the Roller block, grouped by area. Each setting matches a real control in the screen editor.

subarticles.title: Roller section
subarticles.summary: The Roller section configures a spinning wheel picker that captures a visitor's choice — a date, age, size, or similar value — and saves it in a variable you can reuse for personalization or routing. Reach for it when an input has many ordered options that would be too many to show as buttons. It only appears on wheel-picker screens; add one from the canvas, then set the data type, wheels, and label styling here.

subarticles.title: Where it appears
subarticles.summary: Covered screen types: WheelPicker.

subarticles.title: Color of the picker outline
subarticles.summary: Color of the outline around the picker container (default light gray, #E0E0E0). Use a light neutral for a subtle card edge, or your accent color to make the picker stand out on the screen. It only shows when the border thickness above is greater than 0.

subarticles.title: Roundness of the corners
subarticles.summary: How rounded the four corners of the picker container are, in pixels (0-50, default 12). 0 gives sharp square corners; higher values look softer and more modern. Match it to the corner roundness of your buttons and other cards so the whole funnel feels consistent.

subarticles.title: Thickness of the picker outline
subarticles.summary: Width in pixels of the outline around the picker container (0-50, default 1). Set it to 0 for no border and rely on the background color alone, or use 1-2px for a clean, defined edge. The border color setting below only takes effect when this is greater than 0.

subarticles.title: Background behind the wheels
subarticles.summary: Fill color behind the spinning wheels (default white, #ffffff). Choose a color that contrasts enough with the screen background so the picker reads as its own distinct card and the wheel values stay legible. A subtle off-white or light tint often separates the picker from the page better than pure white.

subarticles.title: Space inside the picker
subarticles.summary: Sets the empty space, in pixels, inside the picker container on each side: top, right, bottom, left, between the border and the spinning wheels. The default is usually a small value; increase it to give the wheels breathing room, or keep it tight for a compact picker. A clean, uncluttered picker feels effortless to use, which helps visitors commit their answer and continue through the funnel.

subarticles.title: Text choices or numbers
subarticles.summary: Chooses what the picker collects: String for text choices, which allows up to 5 side-by-side wheels (such as month / day / year), or Integer for a single numeric range (such as age or quantity). Set this first — it limits Integer to one wheel, unlocks up to five wheels for String, and changes how each wheel's options are set up below.

subarticles.title: Pre-selected starting value
subarticles.summary: The value already showing when the screen loads. For List wheels, pick one of your options; for Range wheels, pick any number within the from/to span. Pre-selecting the most common answer reduces friction and prevents accidental empty or extreme submissions — leave it empty only if you truly want nothing chosen up front.

subarticles.title: Size of the selection label
subarticles.summary: Text size of the label that shows the user's current choice above the wheels (0-50, default 18). 16-22 keeps the chosen value clearly readable; very small or 0 effectively hides it. Increase it when you want the selection to stand out as a confirmation of what the user picked.

subarticles.title: Thickness of the label text
subarticles.summary: How heavy the selection label looks, from 300 (Light) to 900 (Black); default 400 (Regular). Use 600-700 (Semibold/Bold) to make the chosen value read as a clear confirmation, or keep it at 400 if it should sit quietly above the wheels. Match it to the weight of your other body text for a consistent look.

subarticles.title: Where the label sits
subarticles.summary: Horizontal position of the selection label within its container: left, center, or right (default center). Center usually lines up with the centered wheels and is the safe choice; switch to left or right only to align the label with other text or a specific layout. This is purely visual and does not change the value the user selected.

subarticles.title: Color of the selection label
subarticles.summary: Color of the label text that shows the user's current choice above the wheels (default black, #000000). Pick a color with strong contrast against the container background so the chosen value stays easy to read, ideally your theme's main text color for consistency. This affects only the label, not the wheel options themselves.

subarticles.title: Edit the wheel's choices
subarticles.summary: The text choices shown on a List-mode wheel. Add, edit, drag to reorder, or delete options (1-20 allowed). The order here is the order users scroll through, so place the most common choices near the top where the starting value lands. Each option is per-language, so translate them if your funnel runs in more than one language.

subarticles.title: Lowest number on the wheel
subarticles.summary: The smallest number a Range-mode wheel starts at. Together with the 'to' value it sets the span users can scroll — for example from 1 to 10 lets them pick any number from 1 through 10. Keep this lower than 'to', and set it to the smallest realistic answer for your question, such as a minimum age or quantity.

subarticles.title: Highest number on the wheel
subarticles.summary: The largest number a Range-mode wheel ends at. Together with the 'from' value it sets the span users can scroll — for example from 1 to 10 lets them pick any number from 1 through 10. Keep this higher than 'from', and set it to the largest realistic answer for your question so users aren't offered absurd values.

subarticles.title: Joiner between wheel values
subarticles.summary: The character or characters used to join selections from multiple wheels into one combined value — for example '/' turns two wheels into 'Large/Red', or a space joins them with a gap. This only matters when you have more than one wheel; leave it as-is for a single-wheel picker. Choose a separator that reads naturally in the answer you'll store and reuse later in the funnel.

subarticles.title: List of options or number range
subarticles.summary: Sets how this wheel's values are built: List means you type each option yourself (sizes, labels, months), while Range means you set a from/to span and the wheel fills in every number between, such as 1 to 10. Use List for arbitrary text choices and Range for evenly-spaced numbers. Note that switching between them clears the options you've already entered for this wheel.

subarticles.title: Add and set up wheels
subarticles.summary: The spinning wheels users scroll to make their choice. Each wheel is either a List of text options or a Range of numbers; use Add Wheel to add more (up to 5 with the String data type, only 1 with Integer), then expand a wheel to set its type, options, and starting value. Each wheel's selection is saved as a variable you can reuse later for personalized copy or to route users down different paths.

subarticles.title: Stepper section
subarticles.summary: The Stepper section builds an auto-advancing progress sequence — timed steps with a moving bar and a title, subtitle, description, and optional image for each step. Use it on 'analyzing' or 'building your plan' screens to hold attention while results are prepared, since that sense of progress lifts how many visitors reach the paywall. It only appears on progress-steps screens; add one from the canvas, then set the total duration and per-step copy here.

subarticles.title: Where it appears
subarticles.summary: Covered screen types: ProgressSteps.

subarticles.title: Split between media and progress
subarticles.summary: Percentage of the screen's vertical space (0-100, default 50%) given to the image/text area; the rest goes to the progress area. Raise it above 50% when your image or step text needs more room, or lower it to make the progress bar more prominent. This appears only for the Image First or Chart First layouts and is hidden for the orbital Circle layout.

subarticles.title: Space around the description
subarticles.summary: Sets the empty space, in pixels, on each side of the step description: top, right, bottom, left. The default is usually 0; add top padding to separate the description from the subtitle above, or side padding to keep multi-line text off the screen edges. Comfortable spacing makes longer copy easy to read, which keeps visitors absorbing your value and tapping through.

subarticles.title: Configure segment description text
subarticles.summary: Text styling for segment descriptions including font size, weight, family, color, line height, and letter spacing. Description text is editable per segment with template variable support.

subarticles.title: Color of the completed portion
subarticles.summary: Color of the filled part of the progress bar that grows as the sequence advances, signaling completion to the user. Defaults to green (#4CAF50). Use your brand accent or a clearly positive color, and keep strong contrast against the empty track so progress reads instantly.

subarticles.title: Space around the image
subarticles.summary: Sets the empty space, in pixels, on each side of the step image: top, right, bottom, left. The default is usually 0; add padding so the image does not touch the title or screen edges and sits balanced in its container. A well-framed visual carries the emotional pull on an ad landing page, so adjust this when the image looks cramped or off-center. This control appears only for the Image First or Chart First layouts.

subarticles.title: Style the step image
subarticles.summary: Controls how each step's image looks: how it scales (fill = cover the box and crop overflow, fit = show the whole image with possible gaps, crop, or tile to repeat), corner rounding, width and height, and tile repeat. Use fit for logos or illustrations you don't want cropped, and fill for photos that should fully cover the box. This appears only for the Image First or Chart First layouts and is hidden for the orbital Circle layout.

subarticles.title: Select progress stepper layout
subarticles.summary: Determines the visual layout for progress steps. Circle displays steps as an orbital arrangement (no image container); Image Container First and Chart Container First show image/text in a container with progress bar. Defines which content elements are shown in each segment (image visibility, title, subtitle, description).

subarticles.title: Space around the progress bar
subarticles.summary: Sets the empty space, in pixels, on each side of the progress bar: top, right, bottom, left. The default is usually 0 for a tight bar that sits close to your content; add top and bottom padding to give it room from the title or image above and below. On an ad funnel a progress bar with a little breathing room reads as a quick, low-effort flow, which keeps people moving forward.

subarticles.title: Space around the subtitle
subarticles.summary: Sets the empty space, in pixels, on each side of the step subtitle: top, right, bottom, left. The default is usually 0; add top padding to set the subtitle off from the title above and bottom padding to separate it from the description below. Adjust it only when the subtitle feels cramped against neighboring text, so the supporting line stays easy to scan and reinforces your pitch.

subarticles.title: Configure segment subtitle text
subarticles.summary: Text styling for segment subtitles including font size, weight, family, color, line height, and letter spacing. Subtitle text is editable per segment with template variable support.

subarticles.title: How thick the progress bar is
subarticles.summary: Height of the filled bar in pixels (0-50, default 4px). 4-8px reads as a clean, modern bar; go thicker only for a bold, attention-grabbing indicator. Set it equal to or greater than the track thickness so the fill sits flush over the track instead of looking sunken.

subarticles.title: How long the progress runs
subarticles.summary: Total time, in seconds (1-120), for the progress sequence to advance through all its steps before the screen continues. Aim for about 4-8 seconds: long enough to feel like real work is happening for the user, short enough to avoid drop-off. Use the play/pause preview to test the pacing against your step text.

subarticles.title: Space around the title
subarticles.summary: Sets the empty space, in pixels, on each side of the step title: top, right, bottom, left. The default is usually 0; add bottom padding to separate the title from the subtitle below, or side padding to keep long titles off the screen edges. A clear, uncrowded title is the first thing visitors read, so the small spacing tweak helps them grasp the offer fast and stay in the funnel.

subarticles.title: Configure segment title text
subarticles.summary: Text styling for segment titles including font size, weight, family, color, line height, and letter spacing. Title text is editable per segment with template variable support (@variable, @link, @countdown).

subarticles.title: Color of the empty track
subarticles.summary: Color of the unfilled part of the progress bar — the portion not yet completed. Defaults to light gray (#E0E0E0), which works for most screens. Keep it clearly lighter than the fill color so the user can read their progress at a glance, or match your page background for a subtler look.

subarticles.title: How thick the empty track is
subarticles.summary: Height of the background track in pixels (0-50, default 4px). Keep it equal to the fill thickness for a standard flat bar — the safe choice for most screens. Make it larger than the fill only if you want a recessed groove look, since mismatched values change how the fill sits inside the track.

subarticles.title: Sticky Container — every setting
subarticles.summary: A floating bar pinned to the bottom of a Flexible Layout screen so the main button stays visible and tappable while content scrolls — its background bar (colour, opacity, corner radius, outline), the spacing from the edges and around the button, and whether it holds a standard or purchase button. This guide documents every setting of the Sticky Container block, grouped by area. Each setting matches a real control in the screen editor.

subarticles.title: Sticky Container section
subarticles.summary: The Sticky Container pins one call-to-action button to the bottom of the screen so it stays visible while the visitor scrolls long content. Turn it on for screens where the next-step or buy button would otherwise scroll out of view — long sales copy, feature lists, the paywall — because keeping the button always tappable is one of the simplest ways to lift click-through on paid traffic. Leave it off on short screens that fit without scrolling, where it just adds clutter.

subarticles.title: Where it appears
subarticles.summary: Covered screen types: FlexibleLayout.

subarticles.title: Color of the bar
subarticles.summary: Sets the color of the bar behind the pinned button (appears only when the bar is shown; defaults to white). Match it to your screen or theme background so the bar feels built-in, and make sure it contrasts with the button so the CTA stays the most eye-catching thing on screen. That contrast is what keeps the call-to-action obvious to paid-traffic visitors.

subarticles.title: Outline color
subarticles.summary: Sets the color of the bar's outline (defaults to black; appears only when the outline thickness is above 0 and the bar is shown). Pick a color that frames the bar without competing with the button — a subtle, theme-matched tone usually works best, keeping attention on the CTA itself.

subarticles.title: Outline thickness
subarticles.summary: Sets how thick the outline around the bar is, in pixels (default 0, meaning no outline; only applies when the bar is shown). Add an outline when the bar's color is close to the screen background and you want a crisp edge that separates the CTA from content behind it. Once it is above 0, the border color setting appears so you can style the outline.

subarticles.title: Pinned button label & style
subarticles.summary: Opens an inline card to set everything about the pinned button: its label, where it goes (next screen, or for a purchase button, which product it buys), icon, colors, fonts and shadows. The two things that move conversion most are setting the action correctly so the CTA actually leads somewhere, and writing a short benefit-driven label like 'Start free trial'. Style it to stand out clearly against the bar so it stays the obvious next step.

subarticles.title: What the button does
subarticles.summary: Chooses the pinned button's job: a standard button navigates to the next screen (use it on flow steps like 'Continue'), while a purchase button starts checkout and ties into your paywall products (use it on the paywall). The bar holds one button at a time, so switching type replaces it with a fresh default — your bar styling is kept, but you'll need to re-set the button's label and action.

subarticles.title: Roundness of the bar corners
subarticles.summary: Sets how rounded the bar's corners are, in pixels (default 12, only applies when the bar is shown). The default looks good on most screens; raise it for a softer, pill-like bar or set it to 0 for sharp corners. Match it to your buttons and cards so the bar looks like part of the design rather than an add-on.

subarticles.title: Pin the CTA to the bottom
subarticles.summary: Turns the sticky bar on or off. When on, your main button stays pinned to the bottom and tappable while the visitor scrolls, and the rest of the bar's settings below appear. Turn it on for long or paywall screens so the action never scrolls out of reach (this protects clicks from paid traffic); leave it off on short screens where the button is always in view.

subarticles.title: Spacing from screen edges
subarticles.summary: Sets the gap, in pixels, between the bar and the top, right, bottom and left edges of the screen. Add a little bottom and side spacing so the bar floats just above the edge instead of touching it. This keeps the CTA clear of the phone's home indicator and gesture area, so the button stays comfortably tappable on mobile, where most paid traffic lands.

subarticles.title: How see-through the bar is
subarticles.summary: Sets how transparent the bar's background is, from fully see-through to fully solid (only applies when the bar is shown). Keep it near solid to keep the CTA crisp and readable; lower it for a softer, glass-like look that lets content show through. Avoid going very transparent — if the button blends into scrolling content, visitors may miss it and you lose clicks.

subarticles.title: Space around the button
subarticles.summary: Sets the inner spacing on all four sides between the bar's background and the button inside it. A little padding keeps the button from looking cramped against the edges and gives a comfortable tap target; too much wastes vertical space and shrinks the visible content. Adjust until the button sits centered with even breathing room.

subarticles.title: Show a bar behind the button
subarticles.summary: Adds a solid bar behind the pinned button and unlocks the background color, opacity, border and corner-radius settings. Keep it on in most cases: the bar separates the CTA from content scrolling underneath, so the button stays readable over busy backgrounds. Turn it off only for a clean floating-button look on simple screens where nothing scrolls behind it.
